subject: history
title: The 1911 Revolution: ending the Qing without a finished republic
dek: A New Army mutiny in Wuchang ended the Qing. A bargain with Yuan Shikai named a republic. A constitution that could bind the man with the army did not follow.
text: The 1911 Revolution: ending the Qing without a finished republic A New Army mutiny in Wuchang ended the Qing. A bargain with Yuan Shikai named a republic. A constitution that could bind the man with the army did not follow. 1911–1912 Xinhai is a calendar name for 1911 in the sixty-year cycle. The soldiers who mutinied in Wuchang did not need that name. This lesson looks out from late Qing China. Sun Yat-sen did not command the Wuchang mutiny; he was in the United States raising money. The dynasty ended because Yuan Shikai, who held the Beiyang Army, cut a deal. A republic was proclaimed. A constitution that could bind the man with the army was not secured. Casualty figures that cannot be sourced here are omitted. Qiu Jin’s execution in 1907 is named as earlier anti-Qing work, not retold. History history 1895 Shimonoseki Qing defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War. The Treaty of Shimonoseki ceded Taiwan and forced a large indemnity. The reform-or-revolution argument that follows starts from this shock. 1898–1901 Reform / Boxer The Hundred Days Reform of 1898, then Empress Dowager Cixi’s coup. The Boxer crisis and the Boxer Protocol of 1901 left the court paying indemnities and launching New Policies to save itself. 1905 Exams / Tongmenghui The civil-service examinations were abolished. In Tokyo, Sun Yat-sen, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others formed the Tongmenghui. Minbao became its paper. 1908–09 Puyi Guangxu and Cixi died in November 1908. The child Puyi became the Xuantong Emperor. Prince Chun ruled as regent. Yuan Shikai was retired from high office. May–Sept 1911 Railways The court nationalized locally financed railway projects and took a four-power loan for the Hukuang lines. Sichuan’s railway protection movement followed. Troops were pulled from Hubei toward Sichuan. 10 Oct 1911 Wuchang After an accidental bomb in Hankou the day before, New Army units in Wuchang mutinied, seized the arsenal, and forced Li Yuanhong to front a Hubei military government. 1 Jan 1912 Nanjing Sun Yat-sen, back from overseas, was inaugurated provisional president of the Republic of China in Nanjing. Li Yuanhong became provisional vice-president. 12 Feb 1912 Abdication Empress Dowager Longyu issued the abdication edict for the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor. Yuan Shikai was already the court’s last general and the revolutionaries’ necessary partner. 10 Mar 1912 Beijing Yuan was sworn in as provisional president in Beijing. The capital stayed where his army was. The Provisional Constitution was promulgated the next day. 1913–16 Song / Hongxian Song Jiaoren was shot at Shanghai railway station on 20 March 1913 and died two days later. Yuan’s monarchy attempt of 1915–16 collapsed. He died in June 1916. Warlord years followed. The man later called the father of the Republic read about Wuchang in a newspaper On 10 October 1911 Sun Yat-sen was in the United States raising money among overseas Chinese. He was in Denver, Colorado. A coded telegram from Huang Xing reached him, but he learned that Wuchang had actually risen from an English-language newspaper. He did not sail straight home to take command of a battle he had not directed. He went first to London and Paris to press the powers not to loan new money to the Qing. By the time he reached Shanghai, in late December, the mutiny was already a string of provincial declarations. The later cult of a founding father has to live with that itinerary. Xinhai Revolution Xinhai 1911 Revolution Chinese Revolution of 1911 辛亥革命 Revolution of 1911 The 1911–12 collapse of the Qing dynasty and proclamation of the Republic of China, conventionally dated from the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 to the abdication of 12 February 1912. Xinhai is the year-name in the sixty-year cycle for 1911. Qing Qing dynasty Manchu dynasty Qing court Last imperial dynasty of China, 1644–1912, a Manchu ruling house over a mostly Han empire. Ended by the abdication edict of 12 February 1912. Republic of China ROC the Republic State proclaimed in Nanjing on 1 January 1912. In this lesson it is the 1912 republic, not later governments in Nanjing or Taipei. Wuchang Uprising Wuchang Wuchang mutiny Double Ten Double Ten Day 雙十 武昌起義 New Army mutiny in Wuchang (one of the Wuhan cities) on 10 October 1911. The date is still marked as the Republic of China’s national day. It was not commanded by Sun Yat-sen. Hankou Hankow Han-Keou Treaty-port city across the Yangtze from Wuchang. The accidental bomb of 9 October 1911 went off in the Russian concession here. Now part of Wuhan. Hanyang The third of the Wuhan cities, with Wuchang and Hankou. It fell to the revolutionaries after Wuchang. Wuhan Wuhan cities The triple city of Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang on the Yangtze in Hubei. The 1911 rising is a Wuhan event with Wuchang as the first mutiny. Sun Yat-sen Sun Yat sen Sun Zhongshan 孫中山 孫文 Sun Wen Sun Yatsen Revolutionary organizer (1866–1925), head of the Tongmenghui, provisional president of the Republic of China from 1 January 1912 until he resigned in Yuan’s favour. In Denver during the Wuchang mutiny. Huang Xing Huang Hsing Huang Keqiang 黃興 Keqiang Hunanese revolutionary (1874–1916), co-founder of the Huaxinghui and a principal military organizer of the Tongmenghui. Fought at Wuhan after Wuchang; minister in the Nanjing provisional cabinet. Song Jiaoren Sung Chiao-jen 宋教仁 Revolutionary and parliamentary politician (1882–1913). Helped found the Tongmenghui and later the Kuomintang. Shot at Shanghai railway station on 20 March 1913; died 22 March. Yuan Shikai Yuan Shih-kai Yuan Shi-kai 袁世凱 Yuan Qing official and Beiyang Army commander (1859–1916). Recalled in 1911, brokered the abdication, became provisional president in Beijing on 10 March 1912, and tried to become emperor in 1915–16. Li Yuanhong Li Yuan-hung 黎元洪 New Army officer (1864–1928), not a Tongmenghui plotter, pressed into serving as military governor of Hubei after Wuchang. Provisional vice-president in 1912; later president of the Republic. Puyi Pu Yi Xuantong Xuantong Emperor 宣統 溥儀 Last Qing emperor (1906–1967). Enthroned as a child after 1908. Abdicated, in Longyu’s edict, on 12 February 1912, aged six. Empress Dowager Longyu Longyu Empress Longyu 隆裕 Qing empress dowager (1868–1913) who issued the abdication edict of 12 February 1912 in the child emperor’s name. Empress Dowager Cixi Cixi Tz’u-hsi 慈禧 De facto ruler of the late Qing (1835–1908). Crushed the Hundred Days Reform in 1898, survived the Boxer crisis, and died the day after Guangxu in November 1908. Guangxu Emperor Guangxu Kuang-hsu 光緒 Qing emperor (1871–1908) who backed the Hundred Days Reform of 1898, was confined by Cixi, and died in November 1908. Prince Chun Zaifeng Regent 醇親王 Father of Puyi and prince regent from 1908. Retired Yuan Shikai from high office in 1909; had to recall him in 1911. Kang Youwei Kang Yu-wei 康有為 Scholar-reformer (1858–1927). A leader of the 1898 Hundred Days. In exile he argued for a constitutional monarchy, not a republic. Liang Qichao Liang Ch’i-ch’ao 梁啟超 Writer and reformer (1873–1929), Kang’s most famous student. After 1898 he published from exile for constitutional monarchy and a new citizen, against Sun’s republican program. Qiu Jin Ch’iu Chin 秋瑾 Revolutionary (1875–1907). Studied in Japan, edited a women’s journal in Shanghai, executed in Shaoxing after Xu Xilin’s 1907 Anqing rising. Named here as 1907 anti-Qing work, not retold as a suffrage life. Xu Xilin Hsü Hsi-lin 徐錫麟 Revolutionary (1873–1907) who assassinated the Anhui governor Enming in Anqing in July 1907. The failed rising led to Qiu Jin’s arrest. Sheng Xuanhuai Sheng Hsuan-huai 盛宣懷 Minister of Posts and Communications in 1911. Ordered railway nationalization and signed the Hukuang loan. A chief civilian target of the railway protection movement. Zhao Erfeng Chao Erh-feng 趙爾豐 Qing official who suppressed the Sichuan railway protection movement in Chengdu in September 1911. The crackdown pulled Hubei troops westward. Rui Cheng Jui Cheng 瑞澂 Viceroy of Huguang in October 1911. Fled Wuchang when the New Army mutinied. Xiong Bingkun Hsiung Ping-k’un 熊秉坤 Junior leader in the 8th Engineering Battalion of the Hubei New Army. Among those who started the 10 October mutiny and moved on the Chuwangtai arsenal. Wu Zhaolin Wu Chao-lin 吳兆麟 New Army company officer in Wuchang. Not the original plot’s commander; given field command on 10 October because the mutiny wanted a more senior officer in charge. Peng Chufan 彭楚藩 Hubei revolutionary executed on the morning of 10 October 1911 after the Hankou bomb exposed membership lists. Liu Fuji Liu Fu-chi 劉復基 Hubei revolutionary executed 10 October 1911 after the Hankou lists were seized. Yang Hongsheng Yang Hung-sheng 楊宏勝 Hubei revolutionary executed 10 October 1911 after the Hankou lists were seized. With Peng and Liu, one of the three names the mutiny moved to avenge. Jiang Yiwu Chiang I-wu 蔣翊武 Literary Society leader in the Hubei New Army, designated commander of the planned rising. He escaped the 9–10 October round-up. Sun Wu 孫武 Gongjinhui organizer in Wuhan, injured in the 9 October Hankou explosion while explosives were being prepared. Cai Yuanpei Ts’ai Yuan-p’ei 蔡元培 Scholar and Tongmenghui member (1868–1940). Minister of education in the Nanjing provisional cabinet of January 1912. Wang Chonghui Wang Ch’ung-hui 王寵惠 Jurist (1881–1958). Foreign minister in the first Nanjing cabinet, seated near Sun in the 5 January 1912 photograph. Chen Tianhua Ch’en T’ien-hua 陳天華 Revolutionary writer (1875–1905), in the 1905 Tokyo Minbao group photograph. Died in Japan that year; named here as a Tongmenghui-generation publicist. Zhang Shizhao Chang Shih-chao 章士釗 Writer (1881–1973), in the 1905 Tokyo Minbao photograph with Huang Xing. Wu Tingfang Wu T’ing-fang 伍廷芳 Diplomat and jurist (1842–1922). Represented the revolutionaries in the north–south peace talks that produced Yuan’s presidency and the Qing abdication. Porfirio Díaz Diaz Porfirio Diaz Mexican president and long-time strongman, resigned May 1911. Named as a contemporaneous old regime that fell the same year as Wuchang. Francisco I. Madero Madero Francisco Madero Mexican civilian politician who became president in November 1911 and was killed in February 1913. The unfinished-civilian-republic problem in the same years. Tongmenghui Revolutionary Alliance United League Chinese United League 同盟會 中國同盟會 Secret revolutionary alliance founded in Tokyo on 20 August 1905 by Sun Yat-sen, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others, merging earlier groups including the Xingzhonghui and Huaxinghui. Core of the later Kuomintang. Xingzhonghui Revive China Society 興中會 Anti-Qing society Sun founded in Honolulu in 1894. Later folded into the Tongmenghui. Huaxinghui China Revival Society 華興會 Revolutionary society Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others organized in Hunan, 1903–04. Merged into the Tongmenghui in Tokyo in 1905. Guangfuhui Restoration Society 光復會 Anti-Qing revolutionary society based among Zhejiang and Anhui activists. Qiu Jin and Xu Xilin worked in this stream. Parts of it cooperated with, and sometimes quarrelled with, the Tongmenghui. Minbao Min Bao People’s Journal 民報 Tokyo newspaper of the Tongmenghui, launched 1905. The 1905 studio photograph in this lesson is of Huang Xing with Minbao colleagues. Literary Society Wenxueshe 文學社 Revolutionary group recruiting inside the Hubei New Army. Together with the Gongjinhui it organized the Wuchang rising. Jiang Yiwu was a leading name. Gongjinhui Progressive Association Co-Progress Society 共進會 Revolutionary society with a Yangtze and secret-society base, allied with the Literary Society inside the Hubei New Army. Sun Wu was a Wuhan organizer. New Army Xinjun 新軍 Late-Qing Western-style forces trained under the New Policies. The Hubei units mutinied at Wuchang. Yuan’s Beiyang divisions were the strongest New Army cluster in the north. Beiyang Army Beiyang Peiyang Army 北洋軍 Yuan Shikai’s New Army in north China, the force that could decide 1911–12. After Yuan’s death in 1916 its factions became warlord armies. New Policies Xinzheng late Qing reforms 新政 Qing reform program after 1901: new schools, abolition of the examinations in 1905, New Army, provincial assemblies, a promised constitution. Intended to save the dynasty. It trained the people who could bury it. civil-service examinations examination system keju 科舉 The old path from classical learning to Qing office. Abolished in 1905. After that date, schools, armies, and overseas study became the new ladders. provincial assemblies provincial assembly Consultative bodies seated from 1909 as part of the New Policies. In 1911 assemblymen in many provinces were the civilians who declared against the Qing alongside New Army officers. Railway Protection Movement railway protection Baolu 保路 保路運動 Railway Rights Protection 1911 protest, strongest in Sichuan, against Qing nationalization of locally financed railways and the transfer of rights toward a foreign loan. The Chengdu crackdown pulled Hubei troops west and thinned the Wuchang garrison. Hukuang loan Hukuang Railway Huguang Railway Hukuang four-power loan 1911 foreign loan from British, French, German, and American banks for the Guangdong–Hankou and Sichuan–Hankou railways. The financial instrument behind railway nationalization. Hubei Military Government Hubei military government 鄂軍都督府 The revolutionary regime declared in Wuchang after 10 October 1911, with Li Yuanhong as military governor, using the old provincial assembly building. The 18-star flag photograph in this lesson is taken in front of it. Nanjing Provisional Government provisional government Nanjing government Nanking Provisional Government Revolutionary national government seated in Nanjing from January 1912, with Sun as provisional president, until Yuan took the presidency in Beijing. Provisional Senate Nanjing Senate provisional senate 臨時參議院 Legislature of the Nanjing republic in early 1912. The 1 April photograph shows Sun resigning to it. provisional president Provisional President Title Sun held from 1 January 1912 and Yuan from 10 March 1912. Provisional meant the office was supposed to wait on a full constitution and a proper election. It became the prize. abdication edict Imperial Edict of Abdication abdication 退位詔書 Edict issued by Empress Dowager Longyu on 12 February 1912, announcing the Xuantong Emperor’s abdication and authorizing Yuan to organize a republic. The legal end of the Qing. Articles of Favorable Treatment Favorable Treatment 優待條件 Terms attached to the 1912 abdication: a stipend for the court, continued residence in the Forbidden City for a time, and the rituals of a retired emperor. Abdication as a contract, not a trial. Provisional Constitution Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China 臨時約法 Promulgated 11 March 1912. It sketched a cabinet responsible to a legislature. It did not control Yuan’s army or keep the capital in Nanjing. Kuomintang KMT Nationalist Party Guomindang 國民黨 Party formed in 1912 when Song Jiaoren merged the Tongmenghui with smaller groups for parliamentary elections. Largest bloc in the 1912–13 National Assembly. Not yet the later Leninist party of the 1920s. National Assembly parliament the assembly The elected legislature of 1912–13 in which the Kuomintang won the largest bloc. Song was on his way to it when he was shot. Three People’s Principles Sanmin zhuyi 三民主義 Sun’s public program: nationalism, democracy, and people’s livelihood. A vocabulary for the Tongmenghui, not a drafted constitution in 1912. queue bianzi Manchu queue pigtail 辮子 The braided hairstyle Qing law required of men as a sign of submission to the Manchu dynasty. Cutting it in 1911 was a public way of leaving the old regime. The 7 November photograph in this lesson shows that act. Iron Blood 18-star flag 18-star flag Iron Blood flag eighteen-star flag 鐵血十八星旗 Banner of the Wuchang rising: a ring of eighteen stars for the provinces of China proper. Crossed in front of the Hubei Military Government in the photograph used as this lesson’s thumbnail. Not the later five-color flag of the Republic. Chuwangtai Chuwan Terrace 楚望台 Arsenal in Wuchang seized on the night of 10 October 1911. Taking it gave the mutineers rifles and a chance. Battle of Yangxia Yangxia October–November 1911 fighting around Hankou and Hanyang between revolutionary forces (Huang Xing among the commanders) and Beiyang units. The revolution did not win Wuhan on the battlefield; it won because provinces kept declaring and Yuan bargained. First Sino-Japanese War Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 1894–95 war War of 1894–95 in which Qing forces lost to Meiji Japan. The Treaty of Shimonoseki followed. The before of the 1911 argument. Treaty of Shimonoseki Shimonoseki 1895 treaty ending the First Sino-Japanese War. Taiwan ceded; a large indemnity; Qing influence in Korea broken. The shock that made reform and revolution both thinkable. Hundred Days Reform Hundred Days Wuxu Reform 戊戌變法 June–September 1898 reform edicts under Guangxu, associated with Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. Ended by Cixi’s coup. Boxer Protocol Boxer crisis Boxer Rebellion Boxer indemnity 辛丑條約 1901 settlement after the Boxer crisis: a huge indemnity to the foreign powers and occupation of access routes to Beijing. The New Policies follow from this humiliation. Baohuanghui Protect the Emperor Society 保皇會 Overseas organization of Kang Youwei’s constitutional monarchists after 1898, in argument with Sun’s republicans for the money and loyalty of Chinese abroad. Second Revolution second revolution of 1913 Failed 1913 armed rising by Sun, Huang Xing and others against Yuan after Song’s assassination. Its failure left Yuan free to crush the KMT in parliament. Twenty-One Demands Twenty-One Demands of 1915 Japanese demands on Yuan’s government in 1915. The shortened acceptance still showed how little the new republic could refuse a foreign power. Hongxian Hongxian Emperor Hongxian era Empire of China (1915–16) 洪憲 Era name of Yuan’s attempted monarchy, announced December 1915, cancelled March 1916. The republic’s president tried on a crown and could not make it hold. warlord years warlords warlord era Period after Yuan’s death in 1916 when Beiyang factions and regional armies governed by force. The after of an unfinished republic, not a full later lesson. Agadir Crisis Agadir Panther’s leap July 1911 Franco-German confrontation over Morocco, opened when Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir. The European imperial summer in which the Qing was still taking foreign railway loans. Mexican Revolution Mexican Revolution of 1910 Uprising against Díaz from 1910. Díaz resigned in May 1911; Madero became president that November and was killed in 1913. Named here as a contemporaneous unfinished civilian republic. Forbidden City palace Imperial palace compound in Beijing. Under the Articles of Favorable Treatment the abdicated court was allowed to remain there for a time. Nanjing Nanking Former Ming capital on the Yangtze. Taken by revolutionaries in December 1911; seat of Sun’s provisional government. The failed attempt to keep the national capital here is part of the Yuan bargain. Beijing Peking Beiping Qing capital, and Yuan’s. After 10 March 1912 the republic’s president sat here because the Beiyang Army did. Shanghai railway station Shanghai Railway Station Where Song Jiaoren was shot on 20 March 1913 while boarding a train for Beijing and the new parliament. Denver Denver, Colorado Colorado city where Sun was fundraising in October 1911. He learned of Wuchang from a newspaper there, not from a field headquarters. Russian concession Russian concession of Hankou Foreign-administered zone in Hankou. The 9 October 1911 bomb went off in a revolutionary hideout here, which is why Russian police, then Qing authorities, got the membership lists. four-power consortium China Consortium four-power group British, French, German, and American banks behind the 1911 Hukuang railway loan. The foreign money in the railway crisis. military governor dudu 都督 Title Li Yuanhong took in Hubei after Wuchang: a provincial military head of a declared republic. Other provinces copied the form. Ministry of Posts and Communications minister of Posts and Communications Late-Qing central ministry. Sheng Xuanhuai headed it in 1911 when railway nationalization and the Hukuang loan were pushed through. Ministry of Foreign Affairs Beijing Ministry of Foreign Affairs The Beijing ministry in whose rooms Yuan was photographed with his officers on 10 March 1912 after taking the oath as provisional president. 8th Engineering Battalion Engineering Battalion eighth engineering battalion Hubei New Army unit that opened the Wuchang mutiny on the evening of 10 October 1911 and moved on the Chuwangtai arsenal. Enming En Ming Manchu governor of Anhui, killed by Xu Xilin in Anqing in July 1907. The failed rising led to Qiu Jin’s arrest and execution. Panther SMS Panther German gunboat sent to Agadir in July 1911. The ship that made the Agadir Crisis visible. Fu Sheng Fulong Photography Studio Fu Sheng, Photographer Tianjin studio that made the circa-1900 cabinet card of Yuan Shikai used in this lesson. The printed English line on the mount reads ‘Fu Sheng, Photographer, City North East Wall Street Tientsin.’ Agence Rol French press-photography agency. The 1911 Hankou street photograph in this lesson is an Agence Rol print now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Bibliothèque nationale de France BnF Gallica French national library. Holds the Agence Rol 1911 Hankou photograph (EST EI-13). University of Washington Libraries Chandless Photographs Robert Henry Chandless Photographs Holds the Fu Sheng cabinet card of Yuan Shikai (PH Coll 214.61) used in this lesson. Anqing Anhui city. Site of Xu Xilin’s 1907 rising. Qiu Jin was arrested after it failed. Chengdu Sichuan capital. Center of the 1911 railway protection movement and of Zhao Erfeng’s September crackdown. Hubei Province on the middle Yangtze. Wuchang was its capital. The New Army mutiny of 10 October 1911 began here. Sichuan Szechwan Province whose railway shareholders led the 1911 Railway Protection Movement. The Qing transfer of Hubei troops toward Sichuan thinned the Wuchang garrison. Guangdong–Hankou Canton–Hankou Hankou-Guangdong Railway One of the two Hukuang railway routes whose rights the 1911 foreign loan pledged. Locally backed in Hubei, Hunan, and Guangdong. Sichuan–Hankou Sichuan-Hankou Railway The other Hukuang route. Barely begun, and the line Sichuan shareholders thought they still owned when the court nationalized it. Spaarnestad Photo Dutch picture archive (now with the Nationaal Archief’s collections) that holds the 7 November 1911 queue-cutting photograph. The Dutch caption anachronistically says ‘Guomindong army’; the print is dated 1911, before the Kuomintang existed under that name. Before After 1895 the court tried to save itself; students in Japan learned how to bury it The First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 ended with the Treaty of Shimonoseki. Taiwan was ceded. A large indemnity was due. Korea slipped from Qing suzerainty. The defeat was not only a lost campaign. It showed that a neighboring state which had rewritten its army and schools could beat the empire that still recruited officials by the civil-service examinations. From that shock two programs were argued in public, often by people who had known one another and then split. Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao wanted a constitutional monarchy under the Guangxu Emperor. In 1898 they had a hundred days of edicts — the Hundred Days Reform — before Empress Dowager Cixi staged a coup, confined Guangxu, and drove the reformers overseas. In exile they organized to protect the emperor, not to kill the dynasty. Sun Yat-sen had already chosen the other door. A commoner schooled in Hawai‘i and Hong Kong, trained as a physician, he had founded the Xingzhonghui in Honolulu in 1894 after the Qing would not hear his reform petition. Failed risings followed. After 1900 the Boxer crisis and the Boxer Protocol left the court paying another indemnity to the foreign powers and trying, late, to modernize itself in order to survive. Huang Xing (seated, center, hat on his lap) with colleagues of Minbao in Tokyo, 1905. The Commons identification puts Chen Tianhua and Zhang Shizhao in the front row and Song Jiaoren standing at back left. This is the overseas student world in which the Tongmenghui was formed that August: a paper, a studio carpet, and a program to replace the Qing with a republic. Studio group of eight Chinese men in Tokyo, 1905: some in Western suits, some in high-collared tunics; Huang Xing seated at center holding a bowler hat. The New Policies of the 1900s were the court’s answer. The examinations were abolished in 1905, which cut the old path from classical study to office. New schools and military academies were opened. Provincial assemblies were promised and, from 1909, seated. A New Army was trained on foreign drill, with Yuan Shikai’s Beiyang divisions as the strongest cluster in the north. None of this was intended to produce a republic. It produced the people who could staff one. Students went to Japan in large numbers. In Tokyo on 20 August 1905, Sun, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others merged older groups — including the Xingzhonghui and Huang’s Huaxinghui — into the Tongmenghui, the Revolutionary Alliance. Minbao carried the arguments. The Three People’s Principles — nationalism, democracy, and a livelihood plank Sun never made into a finished economic program — were the public vocabulary. The work on the ground was also older: secret societies, failed putsches, and women as well as men. Qiu Jin, who had studied in Japan, edited a women’s journal in Shanghai and was executed in 1907 after Xu Xilin’s rising at Anqing. That death belongs in this decade of anti-Qing organizing. It is not a suffrage sequel, and it is not retold here. Guangxu and Cixi died on successive days in November 1908. The child Puyi became the Xuantong Emperor. Prince Chun, his father, served as regent and pushed Yuan Shikai into retirement. The court still talked of a constitution, on a timetable it kept shortening. What it could not do was finish a railway map without foreign money, or keep the New Army’s junior officers from reading the same Tokyo papers as the students. The Xuantong Emperor Puyi as a small child, in a 1910 court photograph. The woman with the Manchu headdress, partly behind the table, is identified as Empress Dowager Longyu. In February 1912 it would be her name, not his, on the abdication edict. The picture is a household still. It is not a government. A small child in Qing court dress sitting on a large chair; to the left, a woman in an elaborate Manchu headdress partly hidden by a table with a vase. The era A railway crisis, an accidental bomb, and a New Army that mutinied without a single hero In the spring of 1911 the Ministry of Posts and Communications, under Sheng Xuanhuai, moved to nationalize locally financed railway projects. A four-power consortium — British, French, German, and American banks — supplied a large loan for the Hukuang lines, the Guangdong–Hankou and Sichuan–Hankou routes that were supposed to tie the interior to the Yangtze. On 9 May the nationalization order went out. Shareholders in Sichuan, who had put provincial money and gentry savings into a railway company that had barely begun to lay track, were offered terms they rejected. The Railway Protection Movement that followed was not a Tongmenghui plot. It was merchants, students, and the provincial assembly against a court that looked as if it were selling the road to foreigners in order to pay old debts. In September the Sichuan authorities, with Zhao Erfeng as the hard edge, broke up the movement in Chengdu. New Army units were ordered in from neighboring Hubei. That transfer thinned the garrison around Wuchang. Hankou, 1911, photographed for the French agency Rol: a street crowd, queues still worn, a porter with tubs, shop signs, and foreign hats in the same frame. Hankou, Hanyang, and Wuchang made up the Wuhan cities on the Yangtze. The uprising began next door in Wuchang. This is the treaty-port street the mutiny did not have to invent. A crowded Hankou street in 1911: a porter with shoulder pole and wooden tubs, men with queues, shop signs in Chinese, and Westerners in pith helmets among the crowd. The men who actually took Wuchang were not Sun’s travelling staff. They were New Army soldiers in Hubei, organized in two overlapping groups, the Literary Society and the Gongjinhui, who had been recruiting inside the ranks. Huang Xing and Song Jiaoren were not in the city. Sun was in the United States. A rising had been discussed for early October, then delayed. On 9 October, in a hideout in the Russian concession of Hankou, someone preparing explosives set off a bomb by accident. The blast brought police. Membership lists were found. Arrests followed. On the morning of 10 October three men — Peng Chufan, Liu Fuji, and Yang Hongsheng — were executed. The remaining plotters inside the barracks could wait to be named from the lists, or they could move. They moved. That evening the 8th Engineering Battalion, with Xiong Bingkun among the junior leaders, mutinied and made for the Chuwangtai arsenal, where other comrades were already posted. Artillery and transport units came over. Wu Zhaolin, a company officer with more rank than the first mutineers, was pushed into field command because a mutiny still wanted a chain of command. The Viceroy, Rui Cheng, fled. By the next day Wuchang was in rebel hands; Hankou and Hanyang followed. There is no single hero in that sequence. There is an accident, a list, three executions, and a garrison that decided not to wait its turn. Revolutionary troops at the Wuchang uprising, 1911. Several men wear a white cloth armband on the left sleeve — the field sign used so mutineers could tell one another from loyal units in the same uniform. The photograph is a group of soldiers, not a painting of a named general winning a battle. Soldiers in dark New Army uniforms and peaked caps, some with white cloth armbands on the left sleeve, holding rifles with bayonets; a wooden structure behind them. Posing in front of the Hubei Military Government in Wuchang after the uprising, with the 18-star Iron Blood flags of the rising crossed at the door. The building had been the provincial assembly. The flags are not yet the five-color flag of the Republic. They are the banner of a mutiny that had to look like a government by the next morning. A line of soldiers in light uniforms standing before a two-storey Western-style brick building; two large dark flags with rings of stars are crossed in front of the entrance. A government needed a name the provincial assembly and the city’s merchants would recognize. Li Yuanhong was a New Army brigade commander, popular enough with soldiers, not a Tongmenghui member, and not a plotter of the bomb. He was pressed into serving as military governor of Hubei. The later stories about how reluctantly he accepted are less important than the political fact: the mutineers borrowed a non-revolutionary officer because a republic, even a local one, still had to look like command. Telegrams went out asking other provinces to follow. Through October and November, assemblymen, New Army officers, and gentry in province after province declared against the Qing. The map did not wait for Sun. Li Yuanhong in a republican military uniform, photographed around 1915 — later than the mutiny. In October 1911 he was a New Army officer without a revolutionary party card. The mutineers needed his name on the Hubei government. The later portrait is the career that name made possible. Studio portrait of Li Yuanhong in a dark high-collared military tunic and peaked cap with a star badge, an aiguillette on his right shoulder. Huang Xing reached the Wuhan cities and took a field command in the fighting that followed, the Battle of Yangxia against Beiyang units Yuan was sending south. The revolution did not win that fight on points. It won because other provinces had already peeled away, and because Yuan did not use the Beiyang Army only to restore the court. Nanjing was taken in early December. Delegates from the independent provinces gathered there. Sun, having gone from Denver to London and Paris to argue against new foreign loans to the Qing, reached Shanghai in late December. On 29 December the delegates elected him provisional president. On 1 January 1912, in Nanjing, he was inaugurated and the Republic of China was proclaimed. The calendar of the Republic would number 1912 as Year One. Li Yuanhong was named provisional vice-president. A cabinet sat. Cai Yuanpei took education; Huang Xing was at the center of the military side. The photograph of that first state council is a table, not a constitution. Sun Yat-sen chairs the first cabinet meeting of the Nanjing Provisional Government, 5 January 1912. Huang Xing is among the ministers at the table; so are Cai Yuanpei and Wang Chonghui. The republic at this point is a room in Nanjing and a list of offices. Yuan Shikai’s army is still in the north. Sun Yat-sen seated at the center of a cloth-covered table with other men in dark suits; papers on the table; a lamp hanging above. A revolutionary soldier cutting a man’s queue, 7 November 1911. The Dutch archive that holds the print dates it that day and describes the braid as the Manchu-mandated sign of the old regime. The location is not named beyond China. The act is the point: leaving the Qing could be done with scissors in a street, in the same weeks that provinces were declaring. A man in a dark uniform and peaked cap holding a long braid cut from the head of a younger man in light padded clothing; two older men in robes and skullcaps watch. How it showed up The Yuan bargain, and why a republic was not yet a constitution The court, in panic, recalled Yuan Shikai and put the Beiyang Army in his hands. He fought enough to show he could take Wuhan back, and not enough to restore a child emperor. He negotiated with the revolutionaries through Wu Tingfang and others while squeezing the palace. Sun offered the presidency if Yuan would deliver a republic. Yuan offered the palace survival if it would abdicate. On 12 February 1912 Empress Dowager Longyu issued the abdication edict in the name of the Xuantong Emperor. The Articles of Favorable Treatment promised the court a stipend, the right to remain in the Forbidden City for a time, and the rituals of a retired monarchy. The Qing ended as a contract. Puyi was six. Sun resigned. The photograph on the steps of the Provisional Senate records that resignation, not the January inauguration. On 10 March Yuan was sworn in as provisional president in Beijing, among his officers, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The next day the Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China was promulgated. It described a cabinet responsible to a legislature and a president who was not supposed to be a new emperor. The capital remained Beijing because that was where Yuan’s army lived. Nanjing had been a revolutionary choice. It was not a military fact. “Republic” in 1912 meant: no emperor, a flag, a calendar, a senate, and a general who had not been elected in any popular sense. It did not yet mean a rule that could stop that general. Yuan Shikai after being sworn in as provisional president, 10 March 1912, photographed with staff at the Beijing Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The uniforms and swords are the argument. The republic’s second provisional president is still a Beiyang commander standing in a northern ministry, not a Nanjing legislator. Yuan Shikai standing at the center of a group of officers in high-collared uniforms and boots, some with swords, in a curtained interior; he holds a peaked cap in his right hand. Sun Yat-sen 孫中山 1866–1925 Physician, overseas organizer, head of the Tongmenghui. He spent 1911 on a fundraising circuit in the United States and learned of Wuchang from a newspaper in Denver. Elected provisional president in Nanjing, inaugurated 1 January 1912, he held the office for weeks and then resigned so Yuan would take the Qing down with him. The later cult treats him as founder. The 1911 file treats him as the name a scattered alliance already had, and as the man who could talk to foreign capitals about loans. Sun as provisional president, 1912, in a high-collared tunic. The portrait is an office image, taken after Wuchang, not a field photograph from 10 October. Yuan Shikai 袁世凱 1859–1916 Builder of the Beiyang Army, retired by the regent, recalled to save the dynasty. He saved himself. The abdication is his leverage made into an edict. The presidency in Beijing is his army made into a title. In 1915–16 he tried to become emperor under the era name Hongxian and failed. He died in 1916. The warlord years are what his army became once there was no longer one Yuan to hold it. Yuan Shikai as a Qing official, photographed in Tianjin by Fu Sheng, about 1900. The verso of the University of Washington print calls him viceroy of Zhili, afterwards first president of the Republic. The robe is the career the court recalled in 1911. Song Jiaoren 宋教仁 1882–1913 Tongmenghui organizer, then the man who tried to turn the alliance into a parliamentary party. In 1912 he helped merge the Tongmenghui into the Kuomintang and campaigned for a cabinet that would check the president. The 1912–13 elections gave his party the largest bloc in the new National Assembly. On 20 March 1913 he was shot at Shanghai railway station on his way to Beijing. He died on 22 March, not yet thirty-one. Without him the republic lost the person who had treated the Provisional Constitution as a job, not a decoration. Song Jiaoren, studio portrait from before his death in 1913. The suit is the parliamentary career he was building, not a battlefield costume. Huang Xing had been the military organizer of the Tongmenghui, the man who stood in the Tokyo photographs and later in the Wuhan fighting. He is in the Nanjing cabinet picture. He is not a fourth founder-statue in this lesson because the unfinished republic is clearer in Song’s murder than in another portrait of a general. Li Yuanhong’s career after Wuchang — vice-president, later president — is what happens when a mutiny’s borrowed name stays in politics. Empress Dowager Longyu’s one state act that still matters is the edict. The child on the throne did not write it. Same time elsewhere Mexico’s civilian was not safe either; Europe was still sending gunboats In Mexico the old regime of Porfirio Díaz had already begun to crack in 1910. In May 1911 Díaz resigned. Francisco I. Madero, a civilian who had called for elections, became president that November — the same autumn as Wuchang. In February 1913 he was overthrown and killed. The Mexican Revolution did not end with a finished constitution in 1911 any more than China’s did. The comparison is not a formula about continents. It is the same problem in the same years: removing a long personal regime is not the same work as binding the next man who has troops. Europe, that summer, was still in the gunboat business. In July 1911 Germany sent the Panther to Agadir in a quarrel with France over Morocco — the Agadir Crisis. The Qing court was, at the same moment, borrowing from a four-power banking group to pay for railways it had just seized from its own provinces. The foreign loan and the foreign gunboat were the world in which a Chinese republic had to open. They are contemporaneous facts, not assigned peers. After Song was killed, Yuan tried on a crown, and the army divided The Kuomintang’s showing in the 1912–13 elections made Song Jiaoren the obvious premier of a cabinet that would have narrowed Yuan’s room. The shooting at Shanghai railway station on 20 March 1913 ended that path. Evidence ran toward people around Yuan’s government; Yuan was never put on trial for it. Sun and Huang tried an armed Second Revolution in the summer of 1913 and lost. Yuan banned the party, hollowed out the assembly, and in 1915 accepted Japan’s Twenty-One Demands in a shortened form that still marked how weak the new state was abroad. In December 1915 he announced a monarchy, with 1916 as the Hongxian era. Provinces rebelled. He cancelled the empire in March 1916 and died on 6 June. What remained was the Beiyang Army without Beiyang’s one manager, and a south that had already learned to declare independence. The warlord years are that split made routine. The Republic of China kept its name, its calendar, and, on paper, its offices. It did not keep a monopoly of force. The student movement of 1919 and the later reorganized Nationalist Party would work in that wreckage. They are the next problems, not this lesson. 1911 ended an empire. It did not finish a republic. That unfinished ground is the fact later politics had to stand on. A question A question to keep asking If a mutiny still needed a non-revolutionary officer’s name, and a republic still needed Yuan’s army, what did the word republic actually bind in 1912? Chinese Revolution (1911–12) — Encyclopaedia Britannica Named encyclopedia entry on the mutiny, the railway crisis, Sun’s return, and Yuan’s bargain. A reference article, not a substitute for a monograph. The Chinese Revolution of 1911 — U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian U.S. government historical sketch of the Tongmenghui, Wuchang, and recognition of the Republic. Written from Washington’s file. Retired ‘Milestones’ series; still a named public text. Sun Yat-sen — Encyclopaedia Britannica Biography of the Tongmenghui leader and provisional president. Use it for the overseas career; it will not narrate Wuchang as his field command, because it was not. Yuan Shikai — Encyclopaedia Britannica Biography of the Beiyang commander who took the presidency and later tried to become emperor. Marie-Claire Bergère — Sun Yat-sen (Stanford University Press, 1998) Publisher page for the English translation by Janet Lloyd. A standard critical biography: the myth, the overseas networks, and the man who was in Denver in October 1911. Buy or borrow; this capsule does not paste the book. Joseph W. Esherick — Reform and Revolution in China: The 1911 Revolution in Hunan and Hubei (University of Michigan Press) Publisher page for the study that locates 1911 in late-Qing New Policies, provincial elites, and the New Army, rather than in Sun’s itinerary abroad. First issued by University of California Press in 1976. Gordon H. Chang — “American Influences on Sun Yatsen” (Education About Asia / Association for Asian Studies) Open essay. Useful on Sun’s 1911 U.S. fundraising tour and on learning of Wuchang from a newspaper rather than from a headquarters he commanded. Agence Rol — crowd in a Hankou street, 1911 (BnF / Gallica) French press photograph in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The street, not a battle painting. subject: literature
title: Existentialism (c. 1943–1960): literature after the occupation
dek: After high modernism’s broken sentence came war, occupation, and Liberation. In Paris a press word — existentialism — stuck to novels and plays of situation, to Les Temps modernes, and to a public break between Camus and Sartre.
text: Existentialism (c. 1943–1960): literature after the occupation After high modernism’s broken sentence came war, occupation, and Liberation. In Paris a press word — existentialism — stuck to novels and plays of situation, to Les Temps modernes, and to a public break between Camus and Sartre. c. 1943–1960 “Existentialism” is a later press and classroom label. Sartre and Beauvoir used it; Camus did not accept it as a school name for himself. Gabriel Marcel had already used related language in 1943. This lesson looks out from occupied and post-Liberation Paris — cafés, a magazine, novels and plays of situation — then notices other 1950s literatures that were running at the same time. They are contemporaneous events, not a West-plus-Asia formula. High modernism is the previous Thursday in this archive; it is not repeated here. Literature literature 1938 La Nausée Sartre’s novel appears. A forerunner written before the war that later readers folded into the postwar label. 1942–43 L’Étranger / L’Être et le Néant Camus’s novel (1942). Sartre’s Being and Nothingness (1943). Occupation Paris is the room, not only the theory. 1944 Huis clos / Liberation No Exit premieres at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 27 May. Paris is liberated in August. 1945 Les Temps modernes First issue, October. Named after Chaplin’s Modern Times. A magazine becomes an institution. 1947–49 La Peste / Le Deuxième Sexe Camus’s The Plague (1947). Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949), first serialized in Les Temps modernes. 1951–52 The break Camus’s The Rebel (1951). Francis Jeanson’s review in Les Temps modernes (May 1952); Camus and Sartre exchange open letters (August). Friendship ends in public. 1952–53 Elsewhere / Paris Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952). Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952). Wright’s The Outsider (1953), written in Paris. c. 1960 The label thins Structuralism and other Paris fashions take the prestige slot. The press word goes stale. This lesson stops before a full postmodernism chapter. Les Temps modernes took its name from a Chaplin film When Sartre’s circle settled on a title for their new review in late 1944, they chose Les Temps modernes — Modern Times — after Charlie Chaplin’s 1936 film. The first issue appeared in October 1945, after paper shortages delayed it. The board included Sartre, Beauvoir, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Raymond Aron, Michel Leiris, Albert Ollivier, and Jean Paulhan. A comedy about factory life became the letterhead of a magazine that argued for littérature engagée. The film is still the easier object to name than the paper ration. existentialism Existentialism Press and classroom name for a mid-twentieth-century cluster of novels, plays, and philosophy that treated freedom, situation, and bad faith as public problems. Sartre and Beauvoir used the word; Camus did not accept it as a school label for himself. high modernism Earlier twentieth-century formal experiment — Woolf, Joyce, Eliot, and others — treated in this archive’s Thursday lesson of that name. The immediate literary past before the 1930s political novel and the war. situation Sartre’s theatre and novel term: a concrete set of constraints and choices, not an abstract theme. A play of situation puts characters into a closed room of consequences. theatre of situation theater of situation Sartre’s name for drama built around a concrete dilemma rather than psychological portrait alone. Huis clos is the usual exhibit. engagement littérature engagée litterature engagee committed literature French for commitment: the claim that writing is not neutral. Sartre’s Qu’est-ce que la littérature? and Les Temps modernes made engagement a magazine program. mauvaise foi bad faith mauvaise foi / bad faith Sartre’s bad faith: lying to oneself about freedom or facticity — pretending one has no choice, or pretending one has no past. The café waiter who overplays being a waiter is the classroom example. the absurd absurd absurdity Camus’s word for the clash between the human demand for meaning and a world that does not answer it. Not a synonym for nihilism in his essays. occupation Occupation the Occupation occupied Paris German occupation of France, 1940–44. The political weather for Huis clos, Combat, and the cafés that still had heat. Liberation Libération liberation of Paris The freeing of Paris in August 1944 and the wider end of occupation. The public after against which Les Temps modernes launched. Les Temps modernes Temps modernes Les Temps Modernes Literary-political review founded by Sartre’s circle; first issue October 1945; titled after Chaplin’s Modern Times. Serialized parts of The Second Sex; published the 1952 Camus–Sartre break. Café de Flore Cafe de Flore the Flore Café on Boulevard Saint-Germain. During the Occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir worked there because the upstairs rooms stayed heated when many hotels did not. Les Deux Magots Deux Magots Café opposite the Flore on the Place Saint-Germain-des-Prés side of the boulevard. The other famous terrace; later a tourist address. Saint-Germain-des-Prés Saint-Germain-des-Pres Saint Germain Left-Bank neighborhood around the old abbey church. The cafés, hotels, and Gallimard offices that made the press story of existentialism a place name. Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier Vieux-Colombier Theatre du Vieux-Colombier Theater du Vieux-Colombier Theatre at 21 rue du Vieux-Colombier. Huis clos premiered there on 27 May 1944. Jean-Paul Sartre Sartre Jean Paul Sartre Philosopher and writer (1905–1980). La Nausée (1938), Being and Nothingness (1943), Huis clos (1944), Les Temps modernes. Public face of the label he partly accepted. Simone de Beauvoir Beauvoir de Beauvoir Simone de Beauvoir Writer and philosopher (1908–1986). The Second Sex (1949); novels and memoirs; co-founder of Les Temps modernes. Not only “Sartre’s partner.” Albert Camus Camus Writer (1913–1960). L’Étranger (1942), The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), The Plague (1947), The Rebel (1951). Editor at Combat; broke with Sartre in 1952. Refused the school label “existentialist.” Maurice Merleau-Ponty Merleau-Ponty Philosopher (1908–1961). Phenomenology of Perception (1945); early Temps modernes editor. Adjacent to the literary circle, not a novelist of situation. Jean Genet Genet Writer and playwright (1910–1986). Thief, prisoner, then Gallimard author. Sartre’s long Saint Genet (1952) made him a philosophical exhibit as well as a literary one. Samuel Beckett Beckett Writer (1906–1989). Waiting for Godot (1953 Paris premiere). Adjacent absurdist theatre, not the Sartre school; named because the same years put both on Paris stages. Frantz Fanon Fanon Psychiatrist and writer (1925–1961). Black Skin, White Masks (1952); The Wretched of the Earth (1961) at the edge of this lesson’s dates. Richard Wright Wright American novelist (1908–1960). Native Son (1940); settled in Paris after the war; The Outsider (1953). Named in the 1930s political past and in the Paris years. Ralph Ellison Ellison American novelist (1914–1994). Invisible Man (1952). Jim Crow and Harlem, not Saint-Germain. Francis Jeanson Jeanson Critic and Temps modernes editor. His May 1952 review of The Rebel triggered Camus’s letter to “Monsieur le Directeur.” Raymond Aron Aron Philosopher and journalist (1905–1983). On the first Temps modernes board; later broke with Sartre’s politics. Named as board fact, not as a deep dive. Jean Paulhan Paulhan Editor (1884–1968). Gallimard / NRF figure on the first Temps modernes board. Michel Leiris Leiris Writer and ethnographer (1901–1990). On the first Temps modernes board. Charlie Chaplin Chaplin Filmmaker. Modern Times (1936) gave Les Temps modernes its title. Modern Times Les Temps modernes namesake Chaplin film, 1936. The magazine’s namesake. Gallimard Paris publisher. Issued many of the books in this lesson and housed early Temps modernes offices. Combat Resistance and postwar newspaper. Camus was a leading editorial voice there during and after the Liberation. La Nausée Nausea Sartre novel, 1938. Prewar forerunner; Roquentin’s nausea at contingency. Place it before 1943, not as a Liberation product. L’Être et le Néant Being and Nothingness L'Etre et le Neant Sartre’s Being and Nothingness, 1943. Philosophical treatise written under occupation; bad faith and freedom as technical terms. L’Étranger The Stranger L'Etranger The Outsider (Camus) Camus novel, 1942 (English: The Stranger / The Outsider). Meursault in Algiers; flat prose; a killing on a beach; a trial that moralizes sunlight and manners. Huis clos No Exit Huis Clos Sartre play, premiered 27 May 1944 at the Vieux-Colombier. Three people locked in a room; “Hell is other people.” Le Mythe de Sisyphe The Myth of Sisyphus Myth of Sisyphus Camus essay, 1942 (The Myth of Sisyphus). The absurd as a starting problem, not a slogan on a beret. La Peste The Plague Camus novel, 1947 (The Plague). Oran under epidemic; read then and later as occupation allegory and as plague narrative. Le Deuxième Sexe The Second Sex Le Deuxieme Sexe Beauvoir’s The Second Sex, 1949. Two volumes: history and myth, then lived experience. Method from philosophy and reportage, not only a feminist label. L’Homme révolté The Rebel L'Homme revolte Camus’s The Rebel, 1951. Essay on revolt and limits; attacked Stalinist apologetics; the book Jeanson reviewed. Peau noire, masques blancs Black Skin, White Masks Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks, 1952. Colonial racism as lived psychic situation. Les Damnés de la terre The Wretched of the Earth Les Damnes de la terre Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth, 1961. At the far edge of this lesson’s dates; named only as later edge. The Outsider The Outsider (Wright) Richard Wright novel, 1953, written in Paris. American existential thriller; not Camus’s L’Étranger under another title. Invisible Man Ralph Ellison novel, 1952. Narrator’s invisibility under American racism. Same year as Fanon’s first book; different city. Native Son Wright novel, 1940. Named as 1930s–40s political-novel past, not as the Paris chapter. Homage to Catalonia Orwell’s 1938 account of the Spanish Civil War. Named as 1930s political writing in the Before section. The Grapes of Wrath Steinbeck novel, 1939. Named briefly as 1930s political fiction. George Orwell Orwell British writer (1903–1950). Named for the 1930s political novel/reportage past. John Steinbeck Steinbeck American novelist (1902–1968). Named for The Grapes of Wrath as 1930s political fiction. Angry Young Men angry young men British press label for mid-1950s writers and playwrights — Osborne’s Look Back in Anger (1956) as the usual stage marker. Class anger in London, not Paris cafés. John Osborne Osborne Playwright (1929–1994). Look Back in Anger, Royal Court Theatre, 1956. Look Back in Anger Osborne play, 1956. The Angry Young Men stage date. Royal Court Theatre Royal Court London theatre in Sloane Square. Look Back in Anger premiered there. Abe Kōbō Kobo Abe Abe Kobo Kōbō Abe Japanese writer (1924–1993). The Woman in the Dunes (1962) is just after this lesson’s center; named as a contemporaneous writer working related problems of confinement and absurdity, not as a Sartre disciple. Ōe Kenzaburō Oe Kenzaburo Kenzaburo Oe Ōe Japanese novelist (1935–2023). Early work from the late 1950s; read Sartre as a French literature student. Contemporaneous, not a twin. The Woman in the Dunes Suna no onna Abe novel, 1962. Sand pit as situation. Named at the edge of the dates. structuralism 1960s Paris intellectual fashion — Lévi-Strauss and others — that took prestige as the existentialist label went stale. Named only as After, not as a full lesson. Qu’est-ce que la littérature? What Is Literature? Qu'est-ce que la litterature? Sartre’s What Is Literature?, 1948 (parts earlier in Temps modernes). Engagement as a theory of prose. Saint Genet Saint Genet, Actor and Martyr Sartre’s long 1952 study of Jean Genet. A philosophical biography that made Genet a case. Waiting for Godot En attendant Godot Beckett play; Paris premiere 1953. Absurd theatre adjacent to this lesson. Jim Crow Legal and customary racial segregation in the United States. The American situation behind Invisible Man. Algiers City where L’Étranger is set. French Algeria, not Paris. Oran Algerian city setting of The Plague. Gabriel Marcel Marcel French philosopher (1889–1973). Used “existentialism” as a label in 1943; later distanced himself from Sartre’s atheist version. Existentialism Is a Humanism L’existentialisme est un humanisme Existentialism is a Humanism L'existentialisme est un humanisme Sartre’s public lecture of 29 October 1945, later a short book. The event that made the press word hard to unsay. Virginia Woolf Woolf Novelist named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday, not as a character in 1945 Paris. James Joyce Joyce Novelist named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday. T. S. Eliot Eliot T.S. Eliot Poet named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday. Meursault Narrator of L’Étranger. His sentences refuse the remorse the court wants. Roquentin Narrator of La Nausée. Named because the 1938 novel is the forerunner. Hell is other people L’enfer, c’est les autres L'enfer, c'est les autres English for Sartre’s line in Huis clos: “L’enfer, c’est les autres.” A claim about the gaze, not a slogan against having friends. Phenomenology of Perception Phénoménologie de la perception Phenomenologie de la perception Merleau-Ponty’s 1945 treatise. Named as his main book in these years, not as a novel. Albert Ollivier Ollivier Journalist on the first Temps modernes board. Named because the masthead is the institution. Lévi-Strauss Claude Lévi-Strauss Levi-Strauss Claude Levi-Strauss Anthropologist (1908–2009). Named only as a marker of 1960s structuralism taking the Paris prestige slot. Gordon Parks Parks American photographer (1912–2006). The Harlem newsboy picture in this lesson is his OWI work, May 1943. Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Adam Powell Adam Clayton Powell Harlem congressman and pastor. His People’s Voice tour poster is in the 1943 newsboy photograph. People’s Voice People's Voice Harlem newspaper associated with Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Visible on the newsstand in the Parks photograph. Pittsburgh Courier Major African American newspaper. A clipping is visible behind the 1943 newsboy. Carl Van Vechten Van Vechten Photographer of the 1939 Wright portrait used in this lesson. 28th Infantry Division 28th Division U.S. Army division marching on the Champs-Élysées in the 29 August 1944 photograph. Champs-Élysées Champs-Elysees Champs Elysees Paris avenue in the Liberation parade photograph. Arc de Triomphe Monument at the head of the Champs-Élysées, visible in the 1944 parade photograph. Lucrèce Borgia Lucrece Borgia Victor Hugo play advertised on a 2018 poster at the Vieux-Colombier in this lesson’s theatre photograph. Named because it is in the picture, not because it is existentialist. Victor Hugo Hugo Playwright of Lucrèce Borgia, visible on the 2018 theatre poster. Named because the caption uses the title. Office of War Information OWI U.S. Office of War Information U.S. wartime information agency. Parks’s Harlem photograph is an OWI assignment. Harlem New York neighborhood. Setting for much of Invisible Man and for Parks’s 1943 newsboy photograph. Second Wave second-wave second wave Later Anglo-American feminism, treated in this archive’s Monday lesson of that name. Named only as a later use of The Second Sex, not as this Thursday’s subject. Nobel Prize Nobel Camus received the literature prize in 1957. Sartre refused it in 1964. Named as after-dates, not as the center of 1945. Poinsett U.S. Army Signal Corps photographer credited on the 29 August 1944 Champs-Élysées parade picture. Signal Corps U.S. Army Signal Corps Army Signal Corps U.S. Army photographic unit. Source of the Liberation parade picture. T1980 Wikimedia username of the photographer who took the August 1967 Venice portrait of Sartre used in this lesson. Diego Delso Delso Photographer of the 2022 Saint-Germain-des-Prés church picture. Tom Hilton Photographer of the 2015 Café de Flore window picture. Britchi Mirela Photographer of the 2011 Les Deux Magots terrace picture. Celette Wikimedia photographer of the 2018 Vieux-Colombier entrance picture. Studio Harcourt Paris portrait studio. Its 1945 Camus photograph is often treated as a French collective work; this capsule does not reproduce it. Constance Borde Borde Co-translator, with Sheila Malovany-Chevallier, of the complete English The Second Sex used in current catalogues. Sheila Malovany-Chevallier Malovany-Chevallier Co-translator of the complete English The Second Sex. Matthew Ward Translator of the American English The Stranger listed in this lesson’s read section. BnF Bibliothèque nationale de France Bibliotheque nationale de France Bibliothèque nationale de France. Hosts the Sartre exhibition notes linked under Read. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy SEP Open reference encyclopedia. The existentialism entry is linked under Read. Penguin Random House Publisher catalogue used for legal edition links to The Stranger and Invisible Man. Before A broken sentence, then a political decade, then a war High modernism had already broken the ordinary novel sentence. Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot made time and attention into structure; vernacular Chinese modernism was running in the same years. That work is another Thursday in this archive. What stands between those experiments and the books in this lesson is not a clean handover. The 1930s put politics back into the foreground of fiction and reportage: George Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia (1938), Richard Wright’s Native Son (1940), John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath (1939). Those titles are named here as the immediate literary past, not as a second lesson. Then came defeat, occupation, collaboration, deportation, and camps. By 1944 the question for many French writers was not how to fragment a day on the page. It was what a person was free to do inside a situation that had already chosen them. The abbey church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, photographed in November 2022. The cafés that sold the postwar story sit on the boulevard beside this tower. The cars and the news kiosk are later. The address is the fact. The Romanesque tower and dark spire of the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés above lower stone buildings and a green Paris news kiosk, photographed in 2022. Sartre’s novel La Nausée had already appeared in 1938. It belongs in this lesson as a forerunner, not as a Liberation product. The occupation years then forced the argument into public rooms: heated cafés when hotels were cold, a theatre still open in May 1944, a Resistance paper, and, after August, a city that had to invent what “after” meant. The era Occupied Paris, Liberation, and a press word The trigger is concrete. Under occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir wrote at the Café de Flore because the upper floor stayed warm when charcoal and hotel heating failed. Huis clos — No Exit — opened at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier on 27 May 1944, still under German control of the city. Three characters locked in a Second Empire drawing room discover that they are one another’s torture. The line everyone remembers, “Hell is other people,” is a situation joke with philosophical teeth, not a poster about hating company. In August the city was liberated. The photographs of soldiers on the Champs-Élysées are the public fact. The literary fact is what a circle of writers did with the next fifteen years. Café de Flore, photographed through the window on 4 June 2015. Red banquettes, waiters in long aprons, a pastry case, a no-smoking sticker on the glass. This is the later tourist interior. During the Occupation the same address was a heated workplace for Sartre and Beauvoir. The caption has to say both things. Looking through a café window at red banquettes, arched mirrors, waiters in long white aprons, and a pastry case under warm lamps. Les Deux Magots, Boulevard Saint-Germain, 6 September 2011. The green awning and the name in gold are the postcard. Sartre’s circle also used this terrace; after the war the two cafés became interchangeable in the press. The timestamp in the corner is the photographer’s; the building is older. Sidewalk terrace of Les Deux Magots under a green awning with gold lettering, round tables and woven chairs, a waiter near the door. In October 1945 Les Temps modernes published its first issue. The title came from Chaplin’s Modern Times. Sartre directed; the board included Beauvoir, Merleau-Ponty, Aron, Leiris, Ollivier, and Paulhan. Camus was busy with Combat and was not on that masthead. The magazine serialized fiction and argument, printed Sartre’s claims for littérature engagée, and later carried chapters of Beauvoir’s The Second Sex. It was an institution in the plain sense: an office, a paper ration, a telephone number printed for visitors, and a place where a review could end a friendship in public. Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 21 rue du Vieux-Colombier, September 2018. The gold letters and the dove emblems mark the house where Huis clos premiered on 27 May 1944. The scooter, the Lucrèce Borgia poster, and the red lobby light are later. The address is the 1944 fact. Street entrance of the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier with gold lettering, a dark modern canopy, red light inside the glass doors, a parked scooter and pedestrians. The word “existentialism” itself was partly a journalist’s convenience. Gabriel Marcel had used related language in 1943. On 29 October 1945 Sartre gave the lecture later published as Existentialism Is a Humanism; the room was crowded enough that the newspapers treated the word as a brand. Sartre and Beauvoir accepted a version of the name in public; Camus kept saying he was not an existentialist in Sartre’s sense. The useful literary unit is not the beret. It is the novel and the play of situation: a character thrown into a set of constraints — a beach, a plague city, a locked room, a sexed body, a colonized gaze — and forced to choose without a guaranteed script. How it showed up Novels and plays of situation — and three to read slowly Name the shelf without pretending it is one committee. Sartre: La Nausée (1938 forerunner), Being and Nothingness (1943), Huis clos (1944), the Temps modernes editorials, What Is Literature? (1948), Saint Genet (1952). Beauvoir: novels, memoirs, and The Second Sex (1949). Camus: L’Étranger (1942), The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), The Plague (1947), The Rebel (1951). Beside them: Genet’s plays and prose; Beckett’s Waiting for Godot (Paris, 1953), adjacent absurd theatre rather than Sartre’s school; Merleau-Ponty’s philosophy in the same offices; Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952), with The Wretched of the Earth (1961) at the far edge; Richard Wright in Paris writing The Outsider (1953). In Japan, Ōe Kenzaburō was reading French literature and Sartre as a student in the late 1950s; Abe Kōbō’s The Woman in the Dunes (1962) sits just after this lesson’s center and works a confinement problem that later readers filed beside the absurd. Those Japanese names are contemporaneous writers facing related pressures after defeat and occupation — not an assigned Asian twin for a Paris trio. Jean-Paul Sartre 1905–1980 Novelist, playwright, philosopher, magazine director. He made “situation” and “bad faith” into tools a general reader could argue with. The 1967 photograph is not a 1944 document; it is a free portrait of the public man the earlier decade produced. Venice, August 1967 — later than the Occupation café years. The face the cameras kept. Simone de Beauvoir 1908–1986 Philosopher and novelist; co-founder of Les Temps modernes. The Second Sex (1949) is a book of method — history, myth, lived reports — as much as it is a founding feminist text later waves would claim. A clearly free studio portrait from the 1940s is hard to license cleanly; this lesson does not invent one. Albert Camus 1913–1960 Novelist, playwright, Combat editor. The Stranger and The Plague made the absurd and revolt readable as stories. He rejected the school name “existentialist,” then broke with Sartre in 1952 over The Rebel. Studio Harcourt’s 1945 portrait is treated as public domain in France on collective-work grounds; this capsule skips it rather than lean on a thin cross-border claim. Richard Wright 1908–1960 Native Son (1940) belongs to the political-novel past. After the war he lived in Paris, knew Sartre and Beauvoir, and published The Outsider (1953). An American writer in the same cafés, not a French mascot. Carl Van Vechten’s studio portrait, 23 June 1939 — before Wright’s Paris years. The face that Native Son made public. Deepen three objects. First, The Stranger. Camus’s French is short, declarative, and cool: “Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday, I don’t know.” Meursault narrates heat, swimming, sex, and a funeral as if they were weather reports. The killing on the Algiers beach arrives with the same flatness. The trial then invents a moral personality the prose has refused to supply — he did not cry at his mother’s funeral, therefore he is a monster. The book’s force is technical: a style that will not perform the remorse the court demands. That is how the absurd gets into the sentences, not only into an essay. Second, The Second Sex. Beauvoir’s 1949 book is two volumes: how “woman” was made in biology talk, history, and myth, then how girls and women live that making. The famous line — one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman — is a claim about situation and becoming, written by a philosopher who had already co-run a magazine. Later Second Wave feminism would take the book as an ancestor; that reception is real. The book itself is also literature and method: long readings, case descriptions, a refusal to treat “woman” as a timeless essence. Put it beside Huis clos and L’Étranger as a postwar Paris object, not only as a chapter in a feminism syllabus. Third, the Camus–Sartre break. The Rebel appeared in 1951. In May 1952 Francis Jeanson reviewed it harshly in Les Temps modernes. Camus answered with a letter addressed not to Jeanson but to “Monsieur le Directeur” — Sartre. In the August issue Sartre answered at length and with personal heat. The friendship ended in the magazine that had defined their public. The argument was about revolt, history, and Marxism; it was also about who owned the postwar moral microphone. Treat it as a literary-political fact with dates, not as a celebrity feud with no content. Same time elsewhere Other 1950s rooms, not a formula While Paris argued about engagement, other literatures were not waiting for a French cue card. In the United States, Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952) sent a nameless narrator through a Southern college, a Harlem movement, and a basement with 1,369 lights. The book’s problem is American racial invisibility under Jim Crow and Northern hypocrisy. It is not a translation of Being and Nothingness. Gordon Parks’s wartime Harlem photographs — a newsboy before posters for Adam Clayton Powell Jr. and the Pittsburgh Courier — are the visual weather of that American situation, taken a decade earlier and still the right street. Harlem newsboy, May 1943, photographed by Gordon Parks for the U.S. Office of War Information. Posters for Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s People’s Voice tour and a Pittsburgh Courier clipping sit behind him; the OWI serial number is printed at the top of the negative. This is New York under wartime Jim Crow, the American “elsewhere” for Invisible Man — not a Paris café. A young Black newsboy in a wool coat and knit cap stands before a newsstand covered with posters, including one for Adam Powell and People’s Voice; OWI serial number at the top. In Britain, the press found “Angry Young Men” after John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger opened at the Royal Court Theatre in 1956. Class resentment and a kitchen sink are the furniture; Saint-Germain is not. In Japan, writers who had lived defeat and occupation were publishing through the 1950s; Ōe’s early fiction and Abe’s later sand-pit novel are named here as parallel pressures, not as proof that existentialism was universal. Latin American boom novels of the 1960s are later and are not forced into this capsule. After The label thins; the books remain By about 1960 the Paris prestige slot was moving. Structuralism — Lévi-Strauss and the arguments that followed — took the seminar glamour. “Existentialist” became a costume in the newspapers: a jazz cellar, a black sweater, a simplified Sartre. Camus died in a car crash on 4 January 1960. Sartre lived long enough to refuse the Nobel Prize in 1964 and to become a different kind of public monument. The useful after is not yet postmodernism as a full lesson. It is this: the novels and plays still work when the beret joke is gone, and other cities had never needed the beret to write their own situations. If this archive takes another Thursday further on, it will not be to complete a French syllabus. It will be because another year also happened. A question A question to keep asking When a magazine can end a friendship in public, what is literature being asked to do that a private letter cannot? Albert Camus — The Stranger (Penguin Random House catalogue) Legal edition listing for L’Étranger (1942). Buy or borrow a standard translation; this capsule does not paste the novel. Simone de Beauvoir — The Second Sex (Penguin UK catalogue) Catalogue record for the Borde/Malovany-Chevallier translation. Library copies exist; this is not a pirated PDF. Ralph Ellison — Invisible Man (Penguin Random House catalogue) 1952 novel. Same-time American book, not a Paris café scene. Existentialism — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy Open reference essay (Kevin Aho). Philosophy context for the literary label; not a substitute for the novels. Sartre and Camus: An Historic Confrontation — publisher page Edited translations of the 1952 Temps modernes exchange (Jeanson, Camus, Sartre). A map of the break, not a bootleg of Les Temps modernes. BnF — Huis clos (Sartre exhibition note) French national library note: premiere at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 27 May 1944. A date and a cast list, not a full play text.
