Altamont Speedway, on 6 December 1969, was a free Rolling Stones concert in northern California that ended in crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter in front of the stage. KSAN-FM, the San Francisco underground station that had inherited Tom Donahue’s staff from KMPX, put callers on the air the next day. The useful historical point is not a sermon. It is that the ballroom’s security, lights, and door could not be improvised at highway scale. The 1960s festival was already a logistics problem. What remained in the shops was album culture. Rock, as a market category, sold long-playing records, gatefold sleeves, and FM time. Hard rock — louder, riff-based, less interested in the light show — is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier San Francisco nights. That line continues into the next decade. A later reaction would treat the album, the solo, and the festival as the things to refuse. That reaction becomes punk. It is not this lesson. The 1965–69 story ends with a longer song, a larger crowd, and a business that had learned to bill the LP as the work. A question A question to keep asking If the unit of the music changes from a three-minute 45 to a side of an LP, who is being asked to sit still, and who is being paid for the extra time? Monterey Pop (D. A. Pennebaker, 1968) Pennebaker’s documentary of the June 1967 festival. Licensed home-video editions exist; this is the catalogue record, not a bootleg upload of the film. The Beatles — Tomorrow Never Knows (1966) Revolver, recorded at EMI Studios, Abbey Road. Official Beatles/UMG upload of the studio recording. Lennon’s vocal through a Leslie speaker; tape loops in the mix. If the file moves, search the title on the Beatles’ official channel. The Beach Boys — God Only Knows (1966) Pet Sounds, Capitol. Official Beach Boys channel. This upload is a later video cut to the 1966 studio recording, not a 1966 television clip. Jefferson Airplane — White Rabbit (1967) Surrealistic Pillow, RCA. Official audio on the Jefferson Airplane channel. Grace Slick brought the song from her previous group, the Great Society. The Jimi Hendrix Experience — Purple Haze (1967) Official audio, Experience Hendrix/VEVO. UK single 1967; on the US edition of Are You Experienced. Not the Monterey film. Pink Floyd — See Emily Play (1967) UK single, 16 June 1967, the weekend of Monterey. Official Pink Floyd channel. Later added to the US edition of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn. A three-minute underground record, not a ballroom jam. Os Mutantes — Panis et Circenses (1968) YouTube Topic upload provided by Universal Music Ltda from the 1968 Polydor/Philips-family master. Written by Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil; arranged with Rogério Duprat. Not a 1968 television clip. 13th Floor Elevators — You’re Gonna Miss Me (1966) YouTube Topic upload of the International Artists recording, provided by The Orchard. From The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. If it moves, search the title plus International Artists.

subject: feminism
title: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political
dek: After the vote, public feminism turned to housework, sex, pay, and who counted as a woman. A bestseller, small consciousness-raising groups, new laws, and a 1977 Black feminist statement made those private facts into politics.
text: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political After the vote, public feminism turned to housework, sex, pay, and who counted as a woman. A bestseller, small consciousness-raising groups, new laws, and a 1977 Black feminist statement made those private facts into politics. c. 1963–1982 “Second wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name, not what most of the people in this lesson called themselves. The dates are a convenience: The Feminine Mystique (1963) at one end, the Equal Rights Amendment’s extended ratification deadline (30 June 1982) at the other. The United States is the spine because the numbering is. Other countries’ 1960s–70s feminisms are contemporaneous — not copies of an American original. Feminism feminism 1963 Mystique / pay Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique. The Equal Pay Act the same year. A bestseller and a statute; neither was the whole cause. 1966 NOW National Organization for Women founded in Washington, 30 June, after a conference of status-of-women commissions. Friedan first president; Pauli Murray among the founders. 1968 Atlantic City New York Radical Women protest the Miss America pageant, 7 September. Freedom Trash Can. No fire. 1970 Books / strike / Ruskin Sexual Politics; The Dialectic of Sex; Notes from the Second Year; Our Bodies, Ourselves as newsprint; Women’s Strike for Equality, 26 August; first UK Women’s Liberation conference at Ruskin College. 1972–73 Statute / Roe Title IX in the Education Amendments of 1972 (signed 23 June). ERA sent to the states. Ms. magazine. Roe v. Wade decided 22 January 1973. 1977 Combahee / Houston Combahee River Collective Statement (April). National Women’s Conference in Houston (November), and a conservative Pro-Family rally in the same city. 1982 Deadline ERA ratification deadline expires 30 June, three states short. Reagan already in office; Thatcher since 1979. The later names — third wave, intersectionality — are not yet the ones in use. There was no fire on the boardwalk On 7 September 1968, New York Radical Women put bras, girdles, high heels, curlers, and women’s magazines into a “Freedom Trash Can” outside the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City. They asked the city for a permit to burn the contents. The permit was refused: the boardwalk is wood. Nothing was burned. Newspapers, then Art Buchwald’s column, reported a bra-burning anyway. The trash can is the event. The bonfire is the copy. second wave Second Wave second-wave A later Anglo-American label for a span of feminist organizing roughly from the early 1960s through the early 1980s. Most people in it did not use the phrase at the time. It is a later name, not a membership card. doldrums A later name for organized U.S. feminism between the vote and the 1960s: the coalition that had fought for suffrage thinned. It describes one public current going quiet. It does not mean women stopped working, studying, or arguing. the feminine mystique feminine mystique Friedan’s name for the postwar middle-class story that a woman’s fulfillment was husband, children, and house. She treated it as an ideology with a sales force — magazines, advertising, experts — not as a private mood. the problem that has no name Friedan’s phrase in The Feminine Mystique for the dissatisfaction of college-educated housewives who had done what they were told and still felt empty. It named a specific class of unhappiness. It did not name every woman’s. The Feminine Mystique Betty Friedan’s 1963 book, published by W. W. Norton. A survey of her Smith College classmates and a polemic against the house-as-destiny. A public starting point. Not a census of American women. Betty Friedan Friedan American writer (1921–2006). The Feminine Mystique (1963); first president of NOW (1966). She later used the phrase “lavender menace” about lesbians in the movement — a split, not a footnote. Equal Pay Act U.S. statute signed 10 June 1963. It required equal pay for equal work on the basis of sex, with exceptions. A workplace law in the same year as Friedan’s book. Enforcement was another matter. Presidential Commission on the Status of Women status-of-women commissions status of women A federal commission created by John F. Kennedy in 1961; Eleanor Roosevelt chaired it until her death in 1962. State commissions followed. NOW was founded at their Third National Conference in 1966. Title VII Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It barred employment discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The word “sex” is in the statute. Early Equal Employment Opportunity Commission practice did not treat it as equal to race. Civil Rights Act of 1964 Civil Rights Act U.S. civil-rights statute. Title VII is the employment title. The Act is the legal floor many workplace feminists stood on; it is not itself a feminist manifesto. EEOC Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, created to enforce Title VII. NOW’s founding complaint was that the Commission was not treating sex discrimination as a real mandate. NOW National Organization for Women National Organization for Women, founded 30 June 1966 in Washington, D.C. Twenty-eight founders; Betty Friedan first president. A civil-rights-style organization for sex equality: lawsuits, lobbying, later the 1970 strike. Not the same thing as women’s liberation small groups. Pauli Murray Murray American lawyer, writer, and later Episcopal priest (1910–1985). Co-founder of NOW; co-author of its Statement of Purpose. “Jane Crow” was her name for the combined racial and sex caste she had already analyzed. Jane Crow Pauli Murray’s term for the system that constrained Black women by race and sex together — not two separate queues. Statement of Purpose NOW Statement of Purpose NOW’s 1966 founding statement. It begins by defining the organization’s purpose as bringing women into “full participation in the mainstream of American society now.” Pauli Murray helped write it. SNCC Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. A major civil-rights organization of the early 1960s. Several white women who later became women’s-liberation organizers had been trained in its discipline — and in its sex hierarchy. New Left The 1960s student and antiwar left, especially Students for a Democratic Society and related groups. A school for organizing. Also a place many women learned they were expected to type, staple, and wait. Casey Hayden Civil-rights organizer. With Mary King she wrote the 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, naming sex hierarchy inside the movement. Mary King Civil-rights organizer; co-author, with Casey Hayden, of the 1965 SNCC memo “Sex and Caste.” Sex and Caste Memo by Casey Hayden and Mary King, November 1965, circulated in SNCC. It compared the position of women in the movement to a caste. A document from inside civil rights, before NOW’s founding conference. consciousness-raising consciousness raising CR CR groups A women’s-liberation method: a small group speaks from its own lives, then looks for the pattern. Kathie Sarachild presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” in 1968. The point was analysis, not therapy — a distinction Carol Hanisch had to keep defending. Kathie Sarachild Sarachild New York Radical Women member. She presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” at the first national women’s-liberation conference, Chicago, November 1968. A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising Kathie Sarachild’s 1968 outline of consciousness-raising as a political method, later printed in Notes from the Second Year. New York Radical Women Early women’s-liberation group, formed in New York in 1967. Among those involved: Shulamith Firestone, Carol Hanisch, Robin Morgan, Kathie Sarachild. It organized the 1968 Miss America protest. the personal is political The Personal Is Political personal is political Phrase attached to Carol Hanisch’s 1969 memo when Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970) and gave it that title. Hanisch has said she did not name the paper. The claim: what gets called a private problem — housework, sex, abortion, shame — is a power relation. Carol Hanisch Hanisch Women’s-liberation organizer; New York Radical Women. She helped organize the 1968 Miss America protest. Her 1969 memo, titled by others in 1970, is the usual source for “the personal is political.” Notes from the Second Year 1970 women’s-liberation anthology edited by Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt. It printed Hanisch’s memo under the title “The Personal Is Political,” and Sarachild’s consciousness-raising program. Anne Koedt Koedt Feminist writer and editor. Co-editor, with Firestone, of Notes from the Second Year. Co-founder of New York Radical Feminists. Shulamith Firestone Firestone Shulie Firestone Writer and organizer (1945–2012). New York Radical Women, Redstockings, New York Radical Feminists. The Dialectic of Sex (1970). Co-editor of Notes from the Second Year. The Dialectic of Sex Shulamith Firestone’s 1970 book (William Morrow). A radical materialist argument: pregnancy and the sex class built on it are the base; cybernetic reproduction is a speculative horizon. Not a NOW pamphlet. Kate Millett Millett Writer and sculptor (1934–2017). Sexual Politics (1970), drawn from her Columbia dissertation: literature and theory as a record of patriarchy. Time put her on a cover; the fame was a trap as much as a platform. Sexual Politics Kate Millett’s 1970 book (Doubleday). Close reading of literary patriarchy — Lawrence, Miller, Mailer, Genet — as political theory. One of 1970’s two brick-sized feminist books; Firestone’s was the other. Redstockings Radical feminist group formed in New York in 1969 (Firestone and Ellen Willis among the founders). Speak-outs, including on abortion. The name plays on “bluestocking” and red. Ellen Willis Writer and critic; co-founder of Redstockings. Later a voice in the late-1970s arguments over sexuality and pornography. women’s liberation women's liberation Women’s Liberation WLM The small-group, often radical current of the late 1960s–70s, distinct from NOW’s organizational liberalism though people crossed. In Britain, Women’s Liberation Movement (WLM) is the usual name. Miss America protest Miss America No More Miss America Demonstration at the Miss America pageant, Atlantic City, 7 September 1968, organized by New York Radical Women. Freedom Trash Can on the boardwalk; a “Women’s Liberation” banner inside the hall. About two hundred people. Not a bonfire. Freedom Trash Can The barrel on the Atlantic City boardwalk, 7 September 1968, into which protesters threw bras, girdles, heels, curlers, and women’s magazines. A permit to burn the contents was denied. Robin Morgan Writer and organizer. A principal organizer of the 1968 Miss America protest; the “No More Miss America” leaflet is associated with her. Later editor of Sisterhood Is Powerful (1970). Sisterhood Is Powerful Anthology edited by Robin Morgan, 1970. A thick reader of the new movement, not a single line. Miss Black America A pageant held in Atlantic City the same night as the 1968 Miss America contest, organized as a Black alternative to a white national symbol. A different project from the boardwalk protest, on the same date. Art Buchwald American humor columnist. After the 1968 Miss America protest he helped spread the bra-burning story that the boardwalk itself had not supplied. Gloria Steinem Steinem Journalist and organizer. A public face of liberal feminism in the 1970s; a founding editor of Ms. magazine (1972). Women’s Action Alliance; National Women’s Political Caucus. Cameras could treat her as the movement. The arguments behind her were already about who “woman” included. Ms. Ms. magazine Ms magazine Feminist magazine. A preview ran in New York magazine in December 1971; the first standalone issue is 1972. Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. “Ms.” as a courtesy title was part of the point. Women’s Action Alliance Women's Action Alliance Organization co-founded in 1971 (Steinem among the founders) to supply practical feminist resources. The 12 January 1972 Leffler photograph of Steinem is from one of its news conferences. National Women’s Political Caucus NWPC National Women's Political Caucus Founded 1971 to elect women and feminist-allied candidates. Among the conveners: Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, Betty Friedan, Gloria Steinem. Bella Abzug Abzug New York congresswoman (elected 1970), lawyer, and a convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Later a co-chair of the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 1977. Shirley Chisholm Chisholm Brooklyn congresswoman, elected 1968 — the first Black woman in the U.S. House. She sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Unbought and Unbossed (1970) is her campaign book and slogan. Unbought and Unbossed Shirley Chisholm’s 1970 book, and the slogan of her campaigns. The phrase is hers, not a later caption. Women’s Strike for Equality Women's Strike for Equality Strike for Equality Actions on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment, called by NOW and joined by a wider coalition. A Fifth Avenue march in New York; sister actions in other cities, including Washington, D.C. Friedan had asked for a strike. What the cameras got was mostly a march. Our Bodies, Ourselves Our Bodies Ourselves Women and Their Bodies Women’s health book that began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. New England Free Press, then a 1973 Simon & Schuster edition. The point was that women could know their own anatomy without waiting for a gatekeeper. Boston Women’s Health Book Collective Boston Women's Health Book Collective Boston Women’s Health Course Collective The Boston group that produced Our Bodies, Ourselves. A workshop, then a pamphlet, then a book that outlived the workshop. Title IX Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June 1972. “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” Sports became the public face. The text is broader. In 2002 the provision was renamed the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act. Education Amendments of 1972 Public Law 92-318, signed by Richard Nixon on 23 June 1972. Title IX is one title inside this law. Nixon’s signing statement did not dwell on the sex-discrimination provision. Patsy Mink Patsy T. Mink Mink Hawaii congresswoman. A principal House advocate of the sex-discrimination provision that became Title IX. The 2002 renaming of Title IX is after her. Birch Bayh Bayh Indiana senator. He introduced the Senate language that became Title IX, 28 February 1972. Richard Nixon Nixon U.S. president who signed the Education Amendments of 1972. The signing statement talked about higher education and busing. It did not sell Title IX as a women’s-sports law. Roe v. Wade Roe Roe v Wade U.S. Supreme Court decision, 410 U.S. 113, announced 22 January 1973. Majority opinion by Harry Blackmun, 7–2. It held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protected a right of privacy broad enough to include a woman’s decision to terminate a pregnancy, structured in trimesters, and struck down Texas’s criminal abortion statute. It was a constitutional holding, not a statute that “legalized abortion.” Overturned in 2022 by Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization. Doe v. Bolton Companion case to Roe, decided the same day (410 U.S. 179). It struck down Georgia’s more elaborate abortion restrictions. Read with Roe, not instead of it. Harry Blackmun Blackmun Supreme Court justice; author of the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade (1973). Equal Rights Amendment ERA Proposed U.S. constitutional amendment: equality of rights shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of sex. Alice Paul introduced an ERA in 1923. Congress sent this version to the states on 22 March 1972. Original deadline 1979; extended to 30 June 1982. It fell three states short of 38. Alice Paul Suffrage organizer; author of the original Equal Rights Amendment introduced in 1923. The 1972 ERA is her text’s descendant. She belongs to the earlier capsule; the amendment did not. Phyllis Schlafly Schlafly Conservative organizer (1924–2016). STOP ERA, from 1972, argued the amendment would strip protections from housewives, send women into the draft, and attack the family. The campaign is a fact of the 1970s, not a later invention. STOP ERA Schlafly’s organization against ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment, from 1972. The stop-sign graphic is the image. The argument was that equality on paper would cost women the legal privileges of marriage and motherhood. Lavender Menace Phrase Betty Friedan used around 1969 for the fear that lesbians would discredit the movement. Reclaimed on 1 May 1970, when Radicalesbians disrupted the Second Congress to Unite Women in New York. The insult became a name. Radicalesbians Lesbian feminist group. They wrote “The Woman-Identified Woman” (1970) and staged the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women, 1 May 1970. The Woman-Identified Woman Radicalesbians manifesto, 1970. It argued that lesbianism was a political position inside feminism, not a public-relations problem for NOW. lesbian feminism A current, not a single organization: the claim that intimate life with women, and a politics built from that fact, was central — not a side issue to be hidden for respectability. Combahee River Collective Combahee Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, 1974–1980. Named for the June 1863 Combahee River Raid, in which Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union expedition that freed hundreds of enslaved people. Their April 1977 statement is the text this capsule slows down for. Combahee River Collective Statement Combahee statement the 1977 statement Dated April 1977. It argues that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression are interlocking, and that Black women’s politics have to start from that fact. It uses the phrase “identity politics” for a coalition that does not require anyone to stand aside. Later printings include a 1979 anthology edited by Zillah Eisenstein. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier. Barbara Smith Writer and organizer; co-founder of the Combahee River Collective; later of Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press. One of the three who later discussed authorship of the 1977 statement. Beverly Smith Organizer and writer; Barbara Smith’s sister; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement. Demita Frazier Frazier Organizer; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement. identity politics In the Combahee statement, a name for politics that begin from one’s own structural position — Black, woman, lesbian, working-class — without treating those as separate queues. The later pejorative use of the phrase is not the 1977 use. Black feminism A current inside the era, not a later correction pasted on. National Black Feminist Organization (1973); Combahee (1974–80); writers including the Smiths, Frazier, and, late in the window, bell hooks. The who-counts problem returning in public. National Black Feminist Organization NBFO Founded in New York in 1973 to address Black women’s position in both the women’s movement and Black politics. Combahee began among Boston women who had been in its orbit and wanted a more radical, socialist, lesbian-inclusive politics. Harriet Tubman Tubman Abolitionist. The Combahee River Collective took its name from the 1863 Combahee River Raid she helped lead. The name is a claim of descent, not a 1970s photograph of her. Combahee River Raid June 1863 Union raid on the Combahee River in South Carolina, with Harriet Tubman as a scout and leader, freeing hundreds of enslaved people. The 1970s collective borrowed the name on purpose. bell hooks hooks Gloria Jean Watkins Writer (Gloria Jean Watkins, 1952–2021). Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (South End Press, 1981). Late in this capsule’s window: she is arguing with a movement that has already named itself, not founding NOW. She kept the name lowercase. Ain’t I a Woman Ain't I a Woman Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism bell hooks’s 1981 book. The title reaches back to Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech — and to the later refrain attached to it. In this archive that refrain’s history is in the First Wave capsule. The 1981 book is about Black women and the feminism that had trouble counting them. National Women’s Conference National Women's Conference Houston conference Houston 1977 Federally funded conference in Houston, 18–21 November 1977, following International Women’s Year. Delegates adopted a National Plan of Action (ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women, and more). Three First Ladies appeared. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in Houston the same weekend. International Women’s Year International Women's Year IWY United Nations designation for 1975. It produced a Mexico City conference and, in the U.S., a commission and the 1977 Houston meeting. National Plan of Action The 26-plank document adopted at Houston in 1977, recommendations to the President and Congress. A federal-conference text. Combahee’s statement, months earlier, is a different kind of “we.” Rosalynn Carter U.S. First Lady in 1977. She appeared at the National Women’s Conference in Houston with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. Betty Ford Former U.S. First Lady; ERA supporter. On the Houston stage, November 1977. Lady Bird Johnson Ladybird Johnson Former U.S. First Lady. On the Houston stage, November 1977, with Rosalynn Carter and Betty Ford. Pro-Family rally Pro-Family Conservative gathering in Houston during the 1977 National Women’s Conference, associated with Schlafly and opponents of the ERA, abortion rights, and lesbian planks. Same city, same weekend, a different “family.” Women Against Pornography WAP Organization founded in New York in 1979. Part of the late-1970s turn toward pornography as a feminist target. The louder “sex wars” continue past this capsule’s 1982 line. MLF Mouvement de libération des femmes Mouvement de liberation des femmes Mouvement de libération des femmes. French women’s-liberation current, named in the press around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. Not a branch office of NOW. Manifesto of the 343 343 Manifeste des 343 Statement published in Le Nouvel Observateur, 5 April 1971, in which 343 women declared they had had abortions, then illegal in France. Simone de Beauvoir was among the signers. Simone de Beauvoir Beauvoir de Beauvoir French philosopher. The Second Sex (1949) is earlier than this capsule. She signed the Manifesto of the 343 in 1971. A predecessor and a contemporary, depending on which book you open. The Second Sex Simone de Beauvoir’s 1949 book (Le Deuxième Sexe). A philosophical inventory of “woman” as Other. It is not a second-wave text; second-wave readers treated it as one anyway. Ruskin College Ruskin Trade-union college in Oxford. Site of the first British National Women’s Liberation Conference, 27 February–1 March 1970. Four opening demands: equal pay, equal education and opportunity, 24-hour nurseries, free contraception and abortion on demand. ūman ribu uman ribu ウーマン・リブ ribu Japanese women’s liberation of the early 1970s, from the English “women’s lib.” Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 pamphlet Liberation from the Toilet is a founding text. Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter, clinic, and meeting place. A critique of the family system and of New Left sexism, not a translation of Friedan. Tanaka Mitsu 田中美津 Japanese ribu organizer and writer. Liberation from the Toilet (便所からの解放), 1970. A founder of the Ribu Shinjuku Center. Liberation from the Toilet 便所からの解放 Benjo kara no kaihō Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 ribu pamphlet. It attacked the treatment of women — including by men on the left — as a receptacle. The title is hers; it is not a metaphor invented for this capsule. Ribu Shinjuku Center リブ新宿センター Ribu Sentā Women’s center and shelter in Shinjuku, Tokyo, 1972–1977. A ribu institution: housing, abortion and legal advice, a paper, a place to go. New Feminism 新女性主義 xin nüxing zhuyi Lü Hsiu-lien’s name for the feminism she promoted in 1970s Taiwan: a 8 March 1972 lecture at National Taiwan University’s law college, then the 1974 book 新女性主義. Slogans included “first a person, then a man or a woman.” This was under martial law, not under the U.S. numbering. Lü Hsiu-lien 呂秀蓮 Annette Lu Lu Hsiu-lien Taiwanese lawyer and writer (b. 1944). She introduced New Feminism in Taipei in the early 1970s after graduate study in the United States. Later vice president of the Republic of China (2000–2008). The later office is not this capsule; the 1974 book is. Stonewall Uprising at the Stonewall Inn, New York, June 1969. Gay liberation is a contemporaneous movement, not a subplot of NOW. Lesbian feminism sits in the overlap. backlash A word later attached, especially by Susan Faludi’s 1991 book Backlash, to the 1980s counter-movement: Reagan–Thatcher conservatism, anti-ERA organizing, a media story that feminism had gone too far. The word is 1991. The conservative turn is already in this lesson’s last years. Susan Faludi Faludi Journalist. Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women (1991). A later name for the 1980s, written after this capsule’s dates. Backlash Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women Susan Faludi’s 1991 book. Useful as a later diagnosis. It is not a 1977 source. Ronald Reagan Reagan U.S. president from 20 January 1981. His first term is the American half of the conservative turn this capsule ends in. Margaret Thatcher Thatcher British prime minister from 4 May 1979. The other English-speaking conservative date in the after. third wave Third Wave third-wave A later name. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” appeared in Ms. in January 1992. This lesson stops before the name. The problems the name tried to hold — race, sexuality, culture, who “we” is — were already on the table. Rebecca Walker Writer. Her 1992 Ms. essay “Becoming the Third Wave” is a usual starting citation for the phrase. It is after this capsule. Becoming the Third Wave Rebecca Walker’s essay in Ms., January 1992. A later christening, not a 1982 event. intersectionality Legal-theoretical name coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 for the way race and sex (and other structures) compound. Combahee had already stated interlocking oppressions in 1977. The word is later. The problem is not. Kimberlé Crenshaw Crenshaw Legal scholar. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) is the usual origin of the word intersectionality. After this capsule; in conversation with it. Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1989 article in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. The named origin of “intersectionality.” Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization Dobbs Dobbs v. Jackson U.S. Supreme Court decision, 2022, that overruled Roe v. Wade. Not part of the 1963–82 span. Named here only as the later fate of a 1973 holding. Levittown Postwar planned suburbs (Pennsylvania, New York, and others) associated with mass-produced houses and a racial boundary at the door. The 1958 photograph in this lesson is a house in Levittown, New York, made for House Beautiful. Architecture as a clue, not a biography of a resident. House Beautiful American shelter magazine. The Gottscho-Schleisner Levittown negatives used here were shot for it in August 1958. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment U.S. constitutional amendment, ratified 1920, barring denial of the vote on account of sex. The 1970 strike chose its fiftieth anniversary. What the amendment did not undo is in the First Wave capsule. First Wave Later label for the suffrage-era public fights already treated in this archive’s Monday lesson of 16 August 2026. The who-counts problem did not end when the vote arrived. John F. Kennedy Kennedy U.S. president who created the Presidential Commission on the Status of Women in 1961. The commissions, not the Oval Office, are the useful fact here. Students for a Democratic Society SDS Major New Left student organization of the 1960s. A training ground and, for many women, a lesson in being asked to type. Chicago Women’s Liberation Union Chicago Women's Liberation Union Socialist-feminist organization founded in Chicago in 1969. Named here as one of the cities that was not New York. Second Congress to Unite Women Feminist conference in New York, 1 May 1970, where Radicalesbians staged the Lavender Menace action. Seneca Falls Village in New York State; 1848 convention site. In 1977 a torch was walked from there to Houston for the National Women’s Conference — a piece of first-wave ceremony reused as second-wave ceremony. Fourteenth Amendment 14th Amendment Ratified 1868. Roe’s majority located a right of privacy in its Due Process Clause. That reading is the 1973 holding; Dobbs rejected it in 2022. Le Nouvel Observateur French weekly. It published the Manifesto of the 343 on 5 April 1971. W. W. Norton Norton New York publisher of The Feminine Mystique in 1963. National Taiwan University NTU Taipei university. Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at its law college on 8 March 1972. George Washington University GWU GWU Women’s Liberation GWU Women's Liberation University in Washington, D.C. Its Women’s Liberation banner is readable in the 26 August 1970 photograph used as this capsule’s hero. LBJ Library LBJ Presidential Library Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library in Austin. Before After suffrage, a quieter movement and a suburban ideal The First Wave (c. 1848–1920) ended, in the United States, with a constitutional sentence about the vote. What followed, in the usual textbook summary, is the doldrums: the suffrage coalition thinned, the Equal Rights Amendment that Alice Paul had already written sat in Congress, and a middle-class public story put women back in the house as if the house were a prize. The word “doldrums” is a later forecast. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that current. Suburban domesticity had an architecture. Mass-produced houses, a car in the drive, a lawn that looked like a job. Magazines sold the picture. So did advertisers and a certain kind of expert. Friedan would call the picture the feminine mystique — a destiny with appliances. The picture was never a map of the country. Black women, working-class women, and anyone who had not been offered the delicate house were already in the workplace, already in other people’s kitchens, already counted as labor. The gap the First Wave left — who counted as the “woman” the movement was picturing — did not close in 1920. It went indoors and called itself normal. Levittown, New York, 28 August 1958: the Mrs. Robert Berman house on Regent Lane, photographed for House Beautiful. The catalog files the resident as a wife of a mailbox. This is the architecture The Feminine Mystique would write against — and it was only ever one class of house. A two-story suburban house in Levittown, New York, with a car in the drive and young trees along a new lawn, 28 August 1958. There was already law at the start of the 1960s. Kennedy’s Presidential Commission on the Status of Women (1961) produced reports and a string of state commissions. The Equal Pay Act arrived in 1963. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 named sex in employment. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission then had to decide whether that word was a mandate or a joke. The school many organizers came out of was not a commission. It was civil rights and the New Left: SNCC, the antiwar movement, Students for a Democratic Society. Casey Hayden and Mary King’s 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, is one document of what women learned there — how to run a meeting, and who was expected to take notes in it. The era A bestseller, consciousness-raising, and laws that reached the workplace and the clinic Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique, published by W. W. Norton in 1963, is the public spark American memory keeps. It is not the cause. Friedan wrote about college-educated housewives and “the problem that has no name.” The book sold because a class of readers recognized themselves. Women who had never been offered that house did not need Friedan to tell them they were tired. Treat the book as a public starting point that magazines could review. Do not treat it as the whole movement. Betty Friedan, 1960 — three years before the book. Fred Palumbo’s World Telegram & Sun portrait is the face later attached to 1963. The useful date in the print is 1960: she is already a public person. The mystique had not yet been a bestseller. Betty Friedan in a 1960 studio portrait, three years before The Feminine Mystique. On 30 June 1966, at the Third National Conference of Commissions on the Status of Women in Washington, twenty-eight people founded the National Organization for Women. Friedan became president. Pauli Murray, who had already named “Jane Crow,” helped write the Statement of Purpose: women into the mainstream of American society now. NOW was built like a civil-rights organization — complaints to the EEOC, lawsuits, lobbying. It was one current. Women’s liberation small groups were another: New York Radical Women (1967), Redstockings (1969), Chicago Women’s Liberation Union, and dozens of unnamed living-room meetings. Consciousness-raising was the method. Kathie Sarachild put it on paper in 1968. You spoke from your own life until housework, sex, pay, and shame stopped looking like a private failure. Carol Hanisch wrote a memo in February 1969 defending those meetings against the charge that they were therapy. When Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970), they titled it “The Personal Is Political.” Hanisch has said the title is theirs. The claim is the era’s: the home was already a political economy. So were abortion, heterosexuality, and the unpaid second shift. How it showed: NOW, and the 26 August 1970 Women’s Strike for Equality on the Nineteenth Amendment’s fiftieth anniversary. Women’s liberation groups that would not be NOW. The Miss America protest of 7 September 1968 in Atlantic City — New York Radical Women, a Freedom Trash Can, a banner inside the hall, men kept off the action, no fire on a wooden boardwalk. The same night, a Miss Black America pageant ran in the same city as a different answer to a white national symbol. Our Bodies, Ourselves began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. Kate Millett’s Sexual Politics and Firestone’s The Dialectic of Sex both arrived in 1970. Ms. magazine’s first standalone issue is 1972; Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. Legislation, in the United States: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June — a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, with Patsy Mink in the House and Birch Bayh in the Senate; sports became the picture people could see. Roe v. Wade, 22 January 1973: a 7–2 Supreme Court, Harry Blackmun writing, held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s due-process privacy covered a woman’s decision to end a pregnancy, with a trimester framework, and struck down Texas’s criminal statute. It was a constitutional holding. It was not a law that “legalized abortion” in a sentence. Doe v. Bolton came down the same day. Gloria Steinem at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. The glasses and the microphone are how a movement got reduced to one person. By 1975 the arguments behind the podium — class, race, lesbianism, who “Ms.” was for — were already the story. Gloria Steinem at a lectern, long hair and aviator glasses, speaking at a women’s conference at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. Black feminism is inside this span, not a footnote written later. The National Black Feminist Organization formed in 1973. The Combahee River Collective, in Boston from 1974, put a statement in April 1977. Lesbian feminism had already refused to wait: Radicalesbians’ “The Woman-Identified Woman,” and the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women on 1 May 1970, answering Friedan’s slur by wearing it. By the late 1970s the arguments were also about pornography and about difference — Women Against Pornography dates to 1979 — and those fights run past the 1982 line this lesson uses as a date, not as a conclusion. Shirley Chisholm announcing a run for the Democratic presidential nomination, 25 January 1972. She had been in the House since 1969. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus, with Steinem, Friedan, and Bella Abzug. Electoral feminism is one street. It is not the only one. Shirley Chisholm in patterned blouse and cat-eye glasses, photographed 25 January 1972 as she announced her presidential candidacy. The field A crowded field, then three things to look at closely A gallery of three portraits is the wrong picture. Name them, then stop treating the names as the era. Friedan, Steinem, Firestone, Millett. Pauli Murray at NOW’s founding. Shirley Chisholm in Congress and on a 1972 ballot. Bella Abzug. Patsy Mink and Birch Bayh on Title IX. Carol Hanisch and Kathie Sarachild on method. Robin Morgan on the boardwalk in 1968. Phyllis Schlafly on the other side of the ERA. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier on a 1977 statement. bell hooks in 1981, late, already arguing with a “women” that had been too small. Tanaka Mitsu in Tokyo. Lü Hsiu-lien in Taipei. The Miss America action as an event that does not belong to one face. Slow down for three, as examples inside the field, not as the field. The Feminine Mystique as a public starting point. Consciousness-raising as a method. Combahee as the who-counts problem returning in public — the same problem the First Wave lesson left unfinished, under a different name. A story Friedan’s book, consciousness-raising groups, and the Combahee statement The book: Friedan gave a class of readers a plot in which their unhappiness was not a personal defect. Magazines could review that plot. Television could book it. NOW could walk through it into the EEOC’s office. The limitation is the same fact as the success. A feminism that begins with a white suburban kitchen will treat everyone else as a later chapter. Working women, Black women, lesbians — they were not later. They were already there, and the usual story did not count them well. The groups: consciousness-raising made a technique out of that omission. You did not begin with a program. You began with what had been called trivia — who does the dishes, who gets believed, who is afraid on the street — and you waited until the trivia had a structure. Hanisch’s memo is the defense of that wait. The New Left had said: those are personal problems; the revolution will fix them; type this stencil in the meantime. CR said the stencil was the revolution’s unfinished business. It could become its own trap: a room of people who already resembled each other, mistaking recognition for a census. The method does not excuse the room. It explains why the room felt like politics. The statement: the Combahee River Collective Statement, April 1977, is not an appendix to Steinem. A Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, named for Harriet Tubman’s 1863 raid, wrote that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression lock together, and that they would not be asked to choose which liberation to stand in line for. “Identity politics,” in their usage, is the opposite of a veto. It is a starting position from which coalition might be possible because no one is required to disappear. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, and Demita Frazier are the three who later talked about writing it. The statement is the collective’s. Four years later, bell hooks’s Ain’t I a Woman (1981) is late in this window on purpose: a book arguing with a movement that had already decided what “woman” sounded like. The title borrows a nineteenth-century question this archive has already complicated. The 1981 argument is new only if you were not listening. Elsewhere Feminism in France, Britain, Japan, and Taiwan in the same years In France the press named a Mouvement de libération des femmes around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. On 5 April 1971, Le Nouvel Observateur printed the Manifesto of the 343: women stating they had had abortions, Simone de Beauvoir among them. The Second Sex was already twenty years old. In Britain, the first National Women’s Liberation Conference met at Ruskin College, Oxford, 27 February–1 March 1970, and listed four demands: equal pay; equal education and opportunity; 24-hour nurseries; free contraception and abortion on demand. In Japan, ūman ribu was not a translation of a New York leaflet. Tanaka Mitsu’s Liberation from the Toilet (1970) went at the family system and at men on the left; the Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter and a clinic. In Taiwan, under martial law, Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at National Taiwan University on 8 March 1972 and published 新女性主義 in 1974: first a person, then a man or a woman. That is a 1970s feminism. It is not an Asian guest at an American table. The same years, in the same cities, were also civil rights, Black Power, the antiwar movement, student revolt, and, after Stonewall in 1969, gay liberation. Women’s liberation came out of those rooms and fought in them. A lesson that treated those movements as background would be repeating the error it is trying to describe. After The ERA failed in 1982, and later writers named a third wave National Women’s Conference, Houston, 19 November 1977. A White House photograph: Rosalynn Carter with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. The banner says WOMAN as if the noun were settled. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in the same city that weekend. Combahee’s statement was already six months old. Stage at the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 19 November 1977, with a WOMAN banner, a torch, and a podium marked National Women’s Conference 1977. Houston in November 1977 is one picture of a peak: a federally funded conference, a National Plan of Action, three First Ladies, a torch walked from Seneca Falls. It is also a picture of a split. The Plan included the ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women. Opponents held their own rally. Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA had been at work since 1972. On 4 February 1977 her people were already at the White House fence with stop-sign stickers. Congress had sent the Equal Rights Amendment to the states in 1972. The deadline, extended, expired on 30 June 1982, three states short of thirty-eight. Phyllis Schlafly, STOP ERA, in front of the White House, 4 February 1977. The smile is part of the politics: a claim that housewives had a movement too. The ERA’s clock was already running. Phyllis Schlafly smiling, a STOP ERA badge on her coat, with other demonstrators and a White House fence behind her, 4 February 1977. Margaret Thatcher took office in May 1979. Ronald Reagan in January 1981. Susan Faludi would call the 1980s a backlash in a 1991 book of that name. The word is later. The conservative turn is in these last years: an official mood that feminism had been tried, or had gone too far, or had been a coastal taste. Roe stood until Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization in 2022. That sentence is outside the era. It belongs here as a fate, not as a twist. The turn into what gets called the third wave is a later naming. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” is 1992, in Ms. Intersectionality, as a word, is Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989. Combahee did not need the word to state interlocking oppressions. The numbered sequence — first the vote, then the rest, then a third period — is the after. It is useful until it hides the people who were never in that sequence. A question A question to keep asking When a movement says the personal is political, whose personal is allowed to count as politics? Roe v. Hanisch’s introduction is the useful correction: she did not title it; Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt did. Combahee River Collective Statement (April 1977) The 1977 text. BlackPast hosts it; the statement itself is the source. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier. It is a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, not a sports law that later grew a statute. title: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a newspaper story that was not the night

text: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a newspaper story that was not the night What diffusion of responsibility claims, then Kitty Genovese, the Times story that launched the teaching example, and the later proof that the story was not what happened on Austin Street. 1964 (and the after of the story) This lesson starts with the concept, not the crime. Catherine “Kitty” Genovese was murdered in Kew Gardens in the early hours of 13 March 1964. The text does not describe wounds or sexual violence. It does not use a police portrait of her or of the killer. The Times story of 27 March 1964 is a primary source that later reporting — including the Times itself in 2016 — found flawed. The psychology that followed is real experimental work. The 38 silent witnesses are not. Psych / soc psych 13 Mar 1964 Kew Gardens About 3:15 a.m.: Genovese is attacked near her apartment off Austin Street. She dies on the way to hospital. 14 Mar 1964 A brief The Times runs a short item. The later front-page story has not been written yet. 27 Mar 1964 “37 Who Saw” Martin Gansberg’s front-page Times story. The headline says 37; the text says 38. None, it claims, called the police. 1968 The lab Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: group size can inhibit helping. They named the mechanism diffusion of responsibility. 2007 The correction Manning, Levine, and Collins in American Psychologist: no evidence for 38 witnesses, or that they watched, or that they all did nothing. 2016 The paper of record The Times calls its 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” An editor’s note is later appended to the online 1964 story. Thirty-seven, or thirty-eight The Times headline of 27 March 1964 counted 37. The story under it counted 38. Reprints have used both. The slip is small and perfect: the number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed. What was stable was the moral — a city that would not pick up the phone. bystander effect Genovese syndrome The finding, from laboratory and field studies after 1964, that people are often less likely to help when others are present. Darley and Latané (1968) are the usual first citation. The effect does not require the Times’s 38 witnesses to be true. diffusion of responsibility Darley and Latané’s term: in a group, each person feels less personally responsible for acting. The more people who could help, the easier it is to assume someone else will. A mechanism tested in labs. Not a transcript of Austin Street. pluralistic ignorance A second mechanism in the helping literature: each person looks at the others, sees no one moving, and concludes the event is not an emergency. Silence reads as information. Kitty Genovese Catherine Genovese Catherine Susan Genovese Born 7 July 1935 in Brooklyn; killed 13 March 1964 in Kew Gardens, Queens, at 28. She managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and lived on Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. The person is older than the newspaper story. Kew Gardens A residential neighborhood in central Queens, around the Long Island Rail Road station and Austin Street. The murder is a Queens story that the Times turned into a story about the city. Austin Street The Kew Gardens street of the apartment and the first attack. Geography, not a set for a play. 38 witnesses thirty-eight witnesses 37 Who Saw The number the 27 March 1964 Times story made famous. The headline said 37; the body said 38. Manning, Levine, and Collins (2007) found no evidence that 38 people witnessed the murder. 37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police 37 Who Saw Murder Didn't Call the Police Martin Gansberg’s New York Times front-page story, 27 March 1964. The article that made the teaching example. The Times later judged it flawed. A. M. Rosenthal Abe Rosenthal Times metropolitan editor in 1964. He later wrote that Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy, over lunch, called the Queens killing “one for the books.” Rosenthal assigned the investigation and, the same year, published Thirty-Eight Witnesses. Murphy New York City police commissioner in 1964. In Rosenthal’s later telling, the lunch remark that started the second-day story. Thirty-Eight Witnesses Rosenthal’s 1964 book on the case. The number, bound as a title. John Darley Social psychologist. With Bibb Latané, “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility” (1968) and The Unresponsive Bystander (1970). Bibb Latané Latane Social psychologist. With John Darley, the 1968 paper and the 1970 book that built the experimental tradition textbooks still teach. Darley and Latané Darley and Latane The usual joint citation for the first bystander experiments. Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968. Group size can inhibit helping. The Unresponsive Bystander Darley and Latané, 1970. The book that named a field. The Genovese story is in the preface; the data are from the lab. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology The APA journal that published the 1968 Darley and Latané paper. Sophia Farrar A neighbor and friend who, after the second attack, went to Genovese, held her, and waited for the ambulance. The newspaper story needed her not to exist. Mary Ann Zielonko Genovese’s partner; they shared the Austin Street apartment. Part of the life the newspaper story flattened into a lesson about strangers. Winston Moseley The man convicted of the murder. This capsule names him once as a fact of the case and does not make him the subject. Robert Mozer A neighbor who shouted during the first attack; Moseley left and later returned. One of the actions the silent-38 story had to erase. McFadden Times reporter; wrote the 4 April 2016 Winston Moseley obituary in which the paper called the 1964 account “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger Author of “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004), an early Times reconsideration. Kitty, 40 Years Later Rasenberger, The New York Times, 8 February 2004. Frances Cherry Psychologist who, with others, later argued that neighbors who heard a man and a woman at 3 a.m. often classified it as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the first parable did not pause for.
