A film, not a primary police file. 9-1-1 911 The U.S. centralized emergency number. In March 1964 New Yorkers reached the police by a precinct number or by dialing the operator. AT&T and the FCC announced a national 911 plan in 1968. urban apathy 1960s press name for the idea that city life makes strangers indifferent. The Genovese story was fitted to it. Ev’s Eleventh Hour The Hollis bar Genovese managed. A job, not a symbol. World’s Fair World's Fair The 1964–65 New York World’s Fair at Flushing Meadows, a few stops from Kew Gardens. Same borough, same spring, a different headline. Civil Rights Act Federal law passed in July 1964. Named here only as a same-year headline, not as a cause of the murder. The New York Times the Times The paper of the 14 March brief, the 27 March story, the 2004 reconsideration, and the 2016 judgment that the 1964 account was flawed. The concept What the bystander effect claims The bystander effect is a claim about groups, not about one Queens street. In its ordinary textbook form it says: a person is less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present. The more potential helpers, the less help. The name that stuck to the mechanism is diffusion of responsibility. Each person feels less personally on the hook. Someone else will call. Someone else is closer. Someone else already knows what this is. That is a statement about psychology. It can be true, false, or true only sometimes. It does not, by itself, require a famous murder, a number of windows, or a city that had forgotten how to be a neighbor. Those arrived later, as a story to hang the claim on. A second, related claim in the same literature is pluralistic ignorance: people treat other people’s inaction as information. If no one moves, the smoke is not a fire. If no one calls, the noise is not a crime. Silence becomes evidence. Diffusion of responsibility is about who must act. Pluralistic ignorance is about whether anything is happening. Textbooks often braid them. They are not the same sentence. The mechanism How Darley and Latané tested helping in a group John Darley and Bibb Latané designed emergencies you could run twice. A subject hears a seizure over an intercom, or sees smoke under a door, alone or with other people present — sometimes other subjects, sometimes confederates who have been told not to move. In 1968, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they reported “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility”: group size inhibited intervention. The 1970 book is The Unresponsive Bystander. The Genovese name is in the preface of a field. The data are from rooms where the experimenters could count. Why did they think it worked that way? Because responsibility, in their account, is not a fixed moral stock. It divides. A person alone owns the next move. A person in a group can wait, look, and assume the waiting is shared. Add the fear of doing the wrong thing in public — of being the one who overreacts — and inaction has two supports: I am not the one, and this may not be the thing. That is the theory. It is a theory about laboratories and, later, field studies. It is not yet a theory about Austin Street. Times Square, May or June 1952 — Angelo Rizzuto, Library of Congress. The 1960s press already had a story about cities as crowds. The bystander experiments gave that story a mechanism. The mechanism did not need a particular sidewalk. Pedestrians, a City Omnibus bus, and stacked billboards on a Times Square sidewalk, about 1952. The parable Kew Gardens, the Times, and the correction The teaching example came from a newspaper. Kew Gardens in 1964 was a Queens neighborhood of brick apartments, a Long Island Rail Road station, and Austin Street shops. Catherine Genovese, 28, managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and shared an apartment at 82–70 Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. There was no 911. A neighbor who wanted the police dialed a precinct or the operator. The city around them had other headlines: a World’s Fair opening in Flushing Meadows; a Civil Rights Act moving through Congress; a press already fond of the phrase urban apathy. Kew Gardens, west to east, about 1936 — Irving Underhill, Library of Congress. A generation before 1964 the neighborhood was already a grid around the railroad. The crime did not invent the place. The later story made the place stand for a whole city. Wide panoramic photograph of Kew Gardens, Long Island, looking west to east, about 1936. In the early morning of 13 March 1964 Winston Moseley attacked Genovese on the Austin Street side of the building. A neighbor, Robert Mozer, shouted; Moseley left and came back. The second attack was in a rear hallway, out of the street’s sight. Later reconstructions — Kevin Cook, the Times in 2016, the 2007 American Psychologist paper — agree on the shape: two attacks, not three; a layout that made a single continuous audience impossible. She was taken away by ambulance and died on the way to the hospital. Sophia Farrar, a neighbor, had gone to her and held her until help came. The station and the south parking lot from Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019. Genovese parked in the railroad lot, about a hundred feet from the apartment door. The cars and the signage are of this century. The cut in the ground is the same fact. Kew Gardens LIRR station and the parking lot south of the tracks, seen from Lefferts Boulevard in 2019. The Times of 14 March ran a short notice. The story that lasted was assigned two weeks later, after Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy told metropolitan editor A. M. Rosenthal, over lunch, that the Queens case was “one for the books.” Martin Gansberg’s piece of 27 March 1964 went on page one: “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police.” The text said thirty-eight. It said they had watched. It said none had called. An unidentified neighbor supplied the line the decade needed: “I didn’t want to get involved.” Rosenthal’s book the same year was Thirty-Eight Witnesses. The alley between the station and Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019 — the ground the case is attached to, in daylight, without a body. It is here as geography, not as evidence of what any window saw. A paved alley and stair from the Kew Gardens LIRR station toward Lefferts Boulevard, photographed in 2019, empty of people. Social psychology moved faster than the corrections. Darley and Latané started from the story the papers had already told. Many textbooks gave the experiments those 38 windows anyway. In 2007, in “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping,” Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins went back to the archive and wrote that there was “no evidence for the presence of 38 witnesses, or that witnesses observed the murder, or that witnesses remained inactive.” The Times, in Robert D. McFadden’s 2016 obituary of Moseley, called the 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger’s “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (2004) had already begun the paper’s own reconsideration. An editor’s note was later appended to the online 1964 story. After What the case still teaches — and what it taught wrongly What it taught wrongly is easy to list. There were not 38 people at 38 windows watching a single continuous crime and choosing, each of them, not to dial. Some neighbors did call. Someone went downstairs. The layout and the two attacks made a single shared audience impossible. Frances Cherry and others later argued that a woman’s voice at 3 a.m. was often classified as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the urban-apathy story did not pause for. James Solomon’s film The Witness records reporters who already doubted Gansberg’s count and did not pick the fight with Rosenthal. The number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed: the headline said 37, the story said 38. What the case still teaches is not a shrug. Some neighbors did too little. The emergency number was a maze. A press story can fit a ready moral — urban apathy, a city of strangers — and become harder to unwrite than to run. The bystander literature is larger than one street and has been tested without Gansberg’s count. The teaching problem is the one this lesson is for: a discipline can be right about a mechanism and still be wrong about the story it uses to make students care. Keep the experiments. Label the newspaper story. Do not let the correction become a second simplification — that no one failed anyone that night, or that groups never freeze a person. Diffusion of responsibility does not need 38 silent windows. It never did. A question A question to keep asking If a field’s most famous example turns out to be a newspaper story that was not the night, what should it do with the example — drop it, label it, or keep using it because the experiment still works? Martin Gansberg — “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police” (The New York Times, 27 March 1964) The article that made the teaching example. Read it as a 1964 front page, then read the 2016 correction. The Times paywall may sit in front of the archive. Robert D. McFadden — Winston Moseley obituary (The New York Times, 4 April 2016) The Times’s own later account, including the judgment that the 1964 story “grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they had perceived.” Manning, Levine, and Collins — “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping” (American Psychologist, 2007) The paper that named the 38-witness story a parable. Abstract and DOI are public; the PDF may sit behind APA’s gate. Jim Rasenberger — “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004) An early Times reconsideration, forty years on, before the 2007 journal article. NPR / All Things Considered — Kevin Cook, 3 March 2014 Cook, author of a 2014 history of the case, on the police number and the interviews underneath it. WNYC — “An Iconic Murder Helped Create the 911 System” (2014) On the emergency-number afterlife. 911 was a national project; New York’s centralized number arrives later than the murder. The piece is a radio essay, not a statute.

subject: business
title: David and Goliath: how the smaller player wins
dek: Asymmetric competition, judo strategy, disruption, and differentiation — then Honda, Southwest, and Canon as cases, used only for the facts named public sources actually state.
text: David and Goliath: how the smaller player wins Asymmetric competition, judo strategy, disruption, and differentiation — then Honda, Southwest, and Canon as cases, used only for the facts named public sources actually state. frameworks, 1979–2001; cases, 1959– This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a biography of three firms and not a promise that underdogs win. Claims about Honda, Southwest, and Canon are traced to named public pieces: Harvard Business Review essays, an HBS case abstract, and a New York Times anniversary account. Operating statistics that those pages do not state are omitted. “David and Goliath” is a metaphor. It is not a dataset. Business business 1958–59 Small machines Honda Super Cub in Japan; American Honda the next year. Xerox 914: the large copier Xerox would later be slow to leave. 1963 Niceness Honda’s U.S. line: “You meet the nicest people on a Honda.” A different rider than Harley-Davidson’s. 1971 Southwest First Southwest Airlines flights in Texas: point-to-point, not a miniature major. 1979–80 Porter “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy”; then Competitive Strategy and the generic-strategy triad. 1995–96 HBR Bower and Christensen on disruptive technologies (Xerox/Canon in the list); Porter, “What Is Strategy?” (Southwest vs Continental Lite). 1999–2001 Judo Yoffie and Cusumano in HBR; Yoffie and Kwak’s book. Movement, balance, leverage — use the larger rival’s weight rather than matching it. Continental Lite copied the easy pieces In “What Is Strategy?” Porter’s warning is not that Southwest was mysterious. It is that a major could copy a fare, a smile, or a 737 and still fail, because the advantage was the fit among activities — what the major would have to stop doing. Continental Lite is his named exhibit of a partial imitation. A larger airline can borrow one piece of a smaller rival’s system and still be a larger airline with the old system attached. David and Goliath The biblical mismatch: a smaller fighter against a giant. In strategy writing it is a metaphor for asymmetric competition — not a claim that underdogs usually win. asymmetric competition Competing by a different set of activities, customers, or weapons than the incumbent, instead of matching size with size. judo strategy Judo Strategy David B. Yoffie and Mary Kwak’s name (book 2001; with Michael A. Cusumano in HBR, 1999) for using a stronger rival’s size against it: movement, balance, leverage — not a head-to-head trial of strength. David B. Yoffie Yoffie Harvard Business School professor. With Michael A. Cusumano, “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (HBR, January–February 1999); with Mary Kwak, the 2001 book Judo Strategy. Mary Kwak Co-author, with David B. Yoffie, of Judo Strategy (Harvard Business School Press, 2001). Michael A. Cusumano Cusumano MIT Sloan professor; with Yoffie, the 1999 HBR essay “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time.” Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time Yoffie and Cusumano, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999. The public HBR statement of the judo metaphor: fast entrants taking on dominant incumbents without matching them blow for blow. Judo Strategy Yoffie and Kwak, Harvard Business School Press, 2001. Subtitled Turning Your Competitors’ Strength to Your Advantage. Movement, balance, leverage. disruptive innovation disruption disruptive technologies Clayton Christensen’s pattern: a simpler or cheaper offer that incumbents’ best customers do not want yet, which later moves upmarket. The 1995 HBR essay with Joseph L. Bower called these “disruptive technologies.” Clayton Christensen Christensen Harvard Business School professor. With Joseph L. Bower, “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (HBR, January–February 1995); later The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997). Joseph L. Bower Bower Harvard Business School professor; co-author with Christensen of “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave.” Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave Bower and Christensen, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995. Why leading firms stay close to current customers and let newcomers take the offers those customers reject — including, in their list, Xerox and the small copier. The Innovator's Dilemma Christensen’s 1997 book. The classroom name that followed the 1995 essay. This capsule uses the essay, which is the public HBR source. differentiation product differentiation In Michael E. Porter’s generic strategies, competing by being different in a way buyers will pay for — not by being the same thing cheaper. In “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, 1996) he tightens this to a unique activity system and the trade-offs that protect it. Michael E. Porter Porter Michael Porter Harvard Business School professor. “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” (HBR, 1979); Competitive Strategy (1980); “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, November–December 1996). What Is Strategy? Porter, Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996. Operational effectiveness is not strategy. Strategy is a unique position, trade-offs, and fit among activities. Southwest Airlines is one of his exhibits; Continental Lite is the failed copy. How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy Porter, Harvard Business Review, March–April 1979. The five-forces essay: rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers. Competitive Strategy Porter’s 1980 book. The three generic strategies — cost leadership, differentiation, focus — live here. The 1996 essay is the later, tighter public statement this capsule leans on. generic strategies Porter’s 1980 triad: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. A map of positions, not a promise that any one of them wins. Honda Honda Motor American Honda Honda Motor Company. In the U.S. motorcycle market it did not first beat Harley-Davidson at large bikes. It sold small, everyday machines to people who had not been Harley’s customer. Soichiro Honda Co-founder of Honda Motor. The NYT’s 2009 anniversary piece is the public named source this capsule uses for the U.S. entry story. Harley-Davidson Harley The incumbent American motorcycle name: large bikes, a heavyweight identity. The larger rival in the Honda story — strong in a market Honda first declined to contest head-on. Super Cub Honda 50 Honda Super Cub Honda’s small step-through motorcycle (1958 in Japan; sold in the U.S. as a small Honda, sometimes the Honda 50). The machine of a different customer. You meet the nicest people on a Honda Honda’s U.S. advertising line, from 1963. The NYT’s 2009 account calls the approach attacking “with niceness”: a different rider than the existing American motorcycle identity. Honda (A) Harvard Business School case (product 384049, 1983) on Honda’s history and U.S. entry, drawing on an earlier case and the Boston Consulting Group’s motorcycle work. Public abstract on the HBR store page; the full case is paid. Boston Consulting Group BCG Consulting firm. Its 1975 report Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry became the planned-strategy version of Honda’s rise — the version Richard Pascale later argued with. Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry Boston Consulting Group report, 1975, for the British government. The planned, scale-curve telling of Honda that classrooms used before Pascale’s interviews. Richard Pascale Author of “Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda’s Success” (California Management Review, 1984). The Honda Effect: much of what worked in America was improvised after the large bikes failed. Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda's Success Pascale, California Management Review, 1984. Interviews with Honda executives that complicate the BCG story of a deliberate small-bike plan. Honda Effect Classroom name for the fight between a planned Honda (BCG) and an emergent Honda (Pascale). A warning against treating a later success as a strategy that was clear on day one. Southwest Airlines Southwest U.S. airline that, from 1971, flew point-to-point on one aircraft type instead of copying the majors’ hub-and-spoke machine. Porter’s 1996 HBR essay uses it as a system of activities; Continental Lite is the copy that did not fit. Herb Kelleher Cofounder and longtime CEO of Southwest Airlines. Bill Taylor’s HBR remembrance (8 January 2019) is the named public source this capsule uses for the person. The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines Bill Taylor, Harvard Business Review, 8 January 2019. A remembrance, not a case exhibit — used here for the person, not for invented operating numbers. Bill Taylor Cofounder of Fast Company; author of the 2019 HBR piece on Kelleher. point-to-point Flying city to city without forcing a connection through a hub. Southwest’s network idea; the opposite of the majors’ hub-and-spoke. hub-and-spoke The major-airline network: feed traffic through a few hub cities. Efficient for a large system; slow and expensive to copy if you are small and want the plane back in the air. Boeing 737 The aircraft type Southwest standardized on. One type means one training school, one spare-parts list, one way to turn a plane. Porter’s point is the fit, not the airframe as a fetish. Continental Lite Continental Airlines’ 1990s attempt to copy pieces of Southwest. Porter’s 1996 essay uses it as the exhibit of a failed partial imitation: a few activities, not the system. Xerox The incumbent of large, often leased, office copiers after the Xerox 914 (1959). Bower and Christensen’s 1995 HBR essay: Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market. Xerox 914 Xerox’s 1959 plain-paper copier. The machine that made copying a corporate center, and that made a later small copier look, to Xerox’s best customers, like a toy. Canon Japanese camera and later copier company. In Bower and Christensen’s 1995 list, the firm that created the small-copier market while Xerox stayed with the customers who wanted big machines. incumbent The firm already strong in a market. Strength here is also a constraint: the customers, assets, and habits that make a new offer look small or wrong. For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction New York Times, 12 July 2009. Named anniversary account of American Honda’s U.S. entry: Pico Boulevard, small motorcycles, Harley and the British bikes as the existing taste, “niceness” as the attack. Rita McGrath Columbia strategy professor. Later commentary has used Southwest as a caution about treating a famous case as a finished recipe. Named here as a limit, not as a source for 1971 facts. Grey Advertising The agency associated with Honda’s U.S. “nicest people” campaign. Named as the usual advertising credit; this capsule does not invent the internal memo. Netscape The 1990s browser company in Yoffie and Cusumano’s 1999 HBR examples of a fast entrant meeting a giant. Microsoft The incumbent in that 1999 HBR pairing. An example from their moment, not a third case in this capsule. Harvard Business Review HBR The journal that published the Porter, Christensen/Bower, and Yoffie/Cusumano essays this capsule cites. A magazine, not a method. California Management Review The journal that published Pascale’s 1984 Honda interviews. The other file in the Honda Effect. The New York Times New York Times NYT Publisher of the 12 July 2009 Honda anniversary account used as a named public source. The problem Why matching a larger rival head-on usually fails A smaller player who attacks an incumbent where the incumbent is already strong is usually volunteering to lose. The larger firm has the customers, the dealers, the plant, the brand, and the lawyers. Matching it blow for blow is a trial of strength. Judo, in the martial-art sense Yoffie and Kwak borrow, is the opposite idea: do not oppose strength to strength. Use the other side’s size against it. That is the problem this lesson is for. Not “how to be inspiring.” Not a tour of three beloved companies. The question is narrower: when the other side is larger, where do you stand so that their size becomes slow? The painting is the metaphor, not the evidence. Strategy frameworks exist because the Bible is not a market study. Caravaggio’s David with the head of Goliath. The framework Three strategy tools, each from a named essay Three named tools, from named essays, because a Saturday business lesson that invents a framework is just a slogan. Judo strategy, as David B. Yoffie and Michael A. Cusumano put it in “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999), is how a fast entrant takes on a dominant incumbent without a sumo match. The 2001 book with Mary Kwak spells the principles as movement, balance, and leverage: define a space the larger firm is slow to enter, refuse a tit-for-tat that favors its size, and turn its assets — dealers, legacy product, current customers — into things it cannot abandon quickly. The HBR essay’s examples are of their internet moment (Netscape and Microsoft, among others). The pattern is older than the browser. Disruptive technologies, in Joseph L. Bower and Clayton Christensen’s “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (HBR, January–February 1995), are offers that today’s best customers reject. Leading firms, the essay says, invest aggressively in what those customers already want. They are late to what looks worse on the old scorecard. Bower and Christensen’s list is blunt: “Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market.” The later classroom word is disruption. The 1995 mechanism is the one this lesson uses: the incumbent is strong, therefore slow, because the wrong customers are speaking. Differentiation, in Michael E. Porter’s Competitive Strategy (1980), is one of three generic strategies: be different in a way buyers will pay for, rather than only cheaper. The tighter public statement is “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, November–December 1996). Operational effectiveness is not strategy. Strategy is a unique position, the trade-offs that come from choosing what not to do, and fit among activities. Porter’s Southwest Airlines is not a mood. It is a system. His Continental Lite is what happens when a larger airline copies a few pieces and keeps the rest of the old machine. Product differentiation is one weapon inside that system — a different customer, a different product, a different activity set — not a logo exercise. Read the three together and the pattern is one sentence: do not attack the place the larger firm is already strongest; attack the thing it cannot leave without becoming a different company. Porter’s 1979 essay “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” is the prior question — what industry are you even standing in — before you pick a fight. The cases Three company cases, used only for the facts the sources state Honda versus Harley-Davidson is the small-bike case. The New York Times’s 12 July 2009 anniversary piece, “For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction,” puts American Honda on Pico Boulevard in 1959, facing a market whose available machines were Harley-Davidsons or British bikes. Honda’s larger models did not do the job those riders already had. The Super Cub — the small Honda, the Honda 50 in American speech — did a different job for a different person. The 1963 line “You meet the nicest people on a Honda” is the public face of that choice. The Times calls it attacking with niceness. In framework language: movement into a space Harley’s identity made expensive to enter, and a product differentiated by who was allowed to look normal on it. The Honda story is also a warning about hindsight. The HBS case Honda (A) (384049, 1983) tells the U.S. rise in part through the Boston Consulting Group’s Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry (1975) — a planned, scale-curve Honda. Richard Pascale’s “Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda’s Success” (California Management Review, 1984) is the other file: executives who said they had no strategy beyond seeing whether they could sell something, large bikes that failed on American roads, Super Cubs used as staff transport until strangers asked where to buy them. The Honda Effect is the name of that argument. Use the case. Do not pretend the slide was written in 1959. A first-generation Honda Super Cub. The point is the scale of the machine, not a sales chart. Harley’s strength was a different motorcycle and a different rider. Caption the object; do not invent the volume. A first-generation Honda Super Cub, step-through frame, small engine, 1958 design. Southwest versus the U.S. majors is the activity-system case. First flights in 1971, Texas, Herb Kelleher among the founders. The public abstract of Vijay Govindarajan and Julie Lang’s Southwest Airlines case states the skeleton this lesson is allowed to use: short-haul, point-to-point, a cost structure the majors did not have. Porter’s 1996 essay is the framework reading: one aircraft type, the Boeing 737; a network that did not worship hub-and-spoke; trade-offs a full-service major could not make without wrecking the rest of its system. Bill Taylor’s 2019 HBR remembrance, “The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines,” is for the person, not for a turnaround-minute that this lesson will not invent. Continental Lite, in Porter, is the larger airline that picked up a few of the pieces and kept the old system on. A Southwest Boeing 737–700, photographed later than 1971. The airframe family is the point Porter needs: one type, one way to turn the plane. The livery is of this century. The idea is not. A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737–700 in canyon-blue livery, landing. Canon versus Xerox is the disruption case already named in Bower and Christensen. The Xerox 914 had made large, often leased, plain-paper copying a corporate center. Those customers wanted more of that. A small copier looked like a worse 914. Canon (and, in the wider history, other Japanese firms) made the small machine for offices that did not have a copy center. Xerox’s strength — the installed base, the service revenue, the definition of a serious copier — was the reason to wait. The 1995 essay’s sentence is the claim: Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market. This lesson does not add a unit count the essay does not give. Limits What the pattern does not explain Judo does not mean the small player is wiser. Sometimes the larger firm is right, and the new offer stays a toy. Christensen’s pattern is famous enough to be over-applied: not every cheaper product is a disruptive technology, and not every incumbent who ignores a niche is about to die. Porter’s fit can become a prison; the same activity system that Continental Lite could not copy can, later, be a reason not to change when the industry does. Rita McGrath and others have since used Southwest itself as a caution about treating a case as eternal. That later argument is not this lesson’s exhibit. It is a reminder that a framework is a lens, not a prophecy. Honda’s two files — BCG and Pascale — are the honest ending. A smaller player can win by attacking where the incumbent is strong and therefore slow. A smaller player can also win because a large bike broke, a clerk asked about the cub, and someone at Grey Advertising wrote a line about nice people. Strategy writing after the fact is very good at turning the second story into the first. The job is to keep both stories in view. After The companies changed; the advice is still about not copying a larger rival’s strengths The 1999 HBR judo essay was written for internet time. The 1995 disruption essay was written for disk drives and copiers and excavators. Porter’s 1996 Southwest is a system that later managers have been tempted to unpick. The pattern — do not fight the larger firm where it is already strongest — is what remains worth teaching on a Saturday. The companies are evidence. They are not saints. A question A question to keep asking If the incumbent’s strength is also the reason it cannot move, what would count as evidence that you are the smaller player with a real opening — and not just the next Continental Lite? David B. Yoffie and Michael A. Cusumano — “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999) The public HBR statement of judo strategy. Paywall possible; the title and the claim are on the open page. Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen — “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995) Why incumbents stay with current customers. The open summary names the Xerox/Canon line this capsule uses. Michael E. Porter — “What Is Strategy?” (Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996) Position, trade-offs, fit. Southwest is an exhibit; Continental Lite is the failed copy. Michael E. Porter — “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” (Harvard Business Review, March–April 1979) The five-forces essay. Industry structure before you pick a fight with a Goliath. Honda (A) — Harvard Business School case 384049 (1983) Public abstract: Honda’s history and U.S. entry, drawing on an earlier case and BCG’s motorcycle work. Full text is paid. “For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction” (The New York Times, 12 July 2009) Named anniversary account: Pico Boulevard, small bikes, Harley and the British machines as the existing taste. Bill Taylor — “The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines” (Harvard Business Review, 8 January 2019) A remembrance of Kelleher. Used for the person, not for fleet counts. Vijay Govindarajan and Julie Lang — “Southwest Airlines” (Tuck / HBS-linked case abstract) Public abstract: short-haul, point-to-point, lowest-cost structure in the domestic industry. Not a license to invent turnaround minutes.

title: War of Resistance (1937–45): the war that did not wait for 1939
dek: From the clash at the Marco Polo Bridge to the wartime capital in Chongqing, this is a world war looked at from China, not as Asia’s footnote to Europe.
text: War of Resistance (1937–45): the war that did not wait for 1939 From the clash at the Marco Polo Bridge to the wartime capital in Chongqing, this is a world war looked at from China, not as Asia’s footnote to Europe. 1937–1945 This lesson looks out from China. Europe’s 1939 is contemporaneous, not the frame. “World War II” as a 1939–45 European story leaves 1937–39 as a preface. From Chongqing, 1939 is the year the European war caught up. Nanjing is treated with one careful image of a city after bombing — no corpses as illustration. Casualty figures that cannot be sourced here are omitted. History history 1931–32 Mukden / Lytton Japan seized Manchuria after the Mukden Incident. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission. The full-scale war was still ahead. 1937 Lugou / Shanghai 7 July at the Marco Polo Bridge; the Battle of Shanghai opened in August and made the war visible to foreign cameras. 1937 Nanjing The capital fell in December. Massacre followed. This lesson will not decorate that fact with bodies. 1938–43 Chongqing Wartime capital after the retreat up the Yangtze. Years of bombing. People lived in tunnels. 1939 Europe Germany invaded Poland. A second opening of a world war, not the first. 1945 Surrender / after Japan surrendered. The Chinese civil war did not wait long. Memory became a second fight between states. Europeans named the bridge for a traveler The stone bridge at Wanping is 盧溝橋, the Lugou Bridge. Europeans called it the Marco Polo Bridge because Polo’s Travels describe a fine bridge in this region. The 1937 incident entered English under the traveler’s name. The soldiers at Wanping were not fighting over a memoir. They were fighting over a crossing and a railway town. The nickname is a European label that stuck. War of Resistance 抗日戰爭 Second Sino-Japanese War Chinese name for the full-scale war with Japan, conventionally dated from 7 July 1937 to 1945. Some Chinese histories include 1931. This capsule uses 1937–45 as the full-scale span and treats 1931 as the before. Marco Polo Bridge Lugou Bridge 盧溝橋 Lugouqiao Stone bridge over the Yongding River near Wanping, southwest of Beiping. A clash beginning 7 July 1937 became the opening of full-scale war. Europeans had long called it the Marco Polo Bridge. Wanping 宛平 Walled town at the north end of the Lugou Bridge. The 1937 incident is a fight over a railway town and a crossing, not a symbol. United Front Second United Front The uneasy wartime cooperation between the Nationalists (KMT) and the Communists after 1937, following the Xi’an Incident of 1936. A front is not a friendship. It is an agreement about who the enemy is this year. Chongqing Chungking 重慶 Sichuan city that became the Nationalist wartime capital after the fall of Nanjing and the retreat up the Yangtze. Japanese bombing of the city, 1938–43, is one of the long air campaigns of the war. Battle of Shanghai August–November 1937. Urban fighting that made the war visible to foreign concessions and foreign cameras. It did not save Nanjing. Nanjing Massacre Nanking Massacre Rape of Nanking After the city fell in December 1937, Japanese troops killed civilians and disarmed soldiers on a mass scale and committed widespread rape. This capsule names the event and does not illustrate it with bodies. Lytton Commission League of Nations commission, 1931–32, led by Lord Lytton, sent to investigate Japan’s seizure of Manchuria after the Mukden Incident. Its report rejected Japan’s account. Japan left the League. The war of 1937 still came. Mukden Incident 18 September 九一八 18 September 1931: an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway used by the Kwantung Army as a pretext to seize Mukden (Shenyang) and then Manchuria. The before of 1937. National Revolutionary Army NRA The Nationalist government’s army, commanded in this war by Chiang Kai-shek. Not the only Chinese armed force in the field; the Communists fought as well, under the United Front’s strained roof. Xi’an Incident December 1936: Zhang Xueliang detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an to force a turn from civil war toward resistance against Japan. The Second United Front follows. A kidnapping used as policy. Beiping Peking Beijing The city now called Beijing. In 1937 it was Beiping — “Northern Peace” — because the Nationalist capital was Nanjing. Names in this capsule follow the political geography of the year. Before Japan had already seized Manchuria in 1931 On 18 September 1931 the Kwantung Army used an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway as a pretext to seize Mukden (Shenyang) and then Manchuria. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission. The commissioners walked tracks, took testimony, and produced a report that did not accept Japan’s story. Japan left the League. The occupation stayed. Investigators on a Manchurian railway — the kind of scene the Lytton Commission’s 1931–32 inquiry produced. A League report can name a pretext. It could not put the province back. Men in suits and hats inspecting a railway track in an open landscape. Inside China the 1930s were also a civil war. The Xi’an Incident of December 1936 — Zhang Xueliang detaining Chiang Kai-shek — forced a turn: a Second United Front against Japan. The front was a cease-fire with a shared enemy, not a merger of the Nationalists and the Communists. That is the politics standing behind 7 July 1937. The era The 1937 fighting spread from Wanping to Shanghai, Nanjing, and Chongqing On the night of 7 July 1937 a Japanese unit near the Lugou Bridge claimed a missing soldier and demanded entry to Wanping. Shots followed. The incident did not stay local. By the end of the month Beiping and Tianjin were gone. In August the Battle of Shanghai opened a war that foreign concessions could photograph from their own rooftops. The fighting lasted into November. It did not save Nanjing. Chiang Kai-shek, in the field, looking through binoculars — a wartime command image. The Nationalist state would lose its capital and move the government upriver. The man in the cap is not the whole war. He is the government that had to relocate. Chiang Kai-shek in uniform looking through binoculars, other officers behind him. A civilian pulling a household — chairs, boards, a rocking horse — through a city street. The War of Resistance is a military history. It is also this: millions of people walking inland with what a cart would hold. A man pulling a cart piled with furniture and a child’s rocking horse through a Chinese city street. Nanjing, the capital, fell in December 1937. What followed is the Nanjing Massacre: mass killing of civilians and prisoners, mass rape. This lesson uses one photograph of a city after air attack — rubble, people standing in it, no bodies arranged for the lens. The event does not need a corpse to be believed. If you need numbers, go to the historians who argue over them in public. They are not invented here. A Chinese city after bombing, 1937 — the archive filename places it in Nanjing. People in the frame are standing. This is the one Nanjing image in the lesson: a capital made into a field of rubble, not a gallery of the dead. Civilians standing in a wide field of rubble after the bombing of a Chinese city, 1937. The government went to Chongqing. From 1938 the city was bombed, again and again, for years. People lived in tunnels. The wartime capital is not a footnote to the fall of France. It is where the Republic of China was still a state. A Japanese bomber over a river city, smoke on the ground — the archive identifies the campaign against Chongqing. From the air, a capital is a target set. From the ground, it is a schedule of sirens. A Japanese twin-engine bomber over a river city, smoke plumes on the ground. In September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. From London that is when “the war” begins. From Chongqing it is the year the European war joined a war already two years old. The United Front still held, badly. Zhou Enlai in the Nationalist capital was diplomacy as much as alliance. Xiao Hong, who had already fled the Northeast, died in 1942 in Japanese-occupied Hong Kong — a writer’s war, not a general’s. Zhou Enlai (center) with the American journalist Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao, 1938. The United Front had to be explained to foreigners as well as fought. A photograph of three people standing is not a merger of two parties. Zhou Enlai in a dark suit standing between Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao. People A general, a diplomat, a writer Chiang Kai-shek 蔣介石 1887–1975 Head of the Nationalist government and commander of the National Revolutionary Army. He lost the coast and kept a state in Sichuan. The after of 1945 — civil war, then Taiwan — is also his. Wartime command photograph, looking through binoculars. Zhou Enlai 周恩來 1898–1976 Communist representative in the United Front’s public face. Chongqing and the liaison work are part of how the Chinese Communist Party survived the war as a political fact, not only as a guerrilla force. 1938, with Edgar Snow and Deng Yingchao. Xiao Hong 蕭紅 1911–1942 Born in the Northeast. The Field of Life and Death and a short life lived as a refugee — Wuhan, Chongqing, Hong Kong. She died in 1942. A war of resistance is also a war of people who were not in uniform. Xiao Hong, a 1930s portrait. A story What a refugee cart was carrying In the Shanghai refugee photograph the cart is a household turned into a load. The rocking horse is the detail that makes the load a family. This is not a cute war. It is a reminder that “home front” in this war often meant there was no front that stayed put, and home was something you carried. Europe in 1939 produced its own carts. title: High modernism (c. 1910–30): writers break the ordinary sentence
dek: Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot changed how a novel or a poem could move through time. In the same years, the magazine 新青年 and Lu Xun changed the written language of Chinese literature. They are contemporaneous events, not a required pairing.
text: High modernism (c. 1910–30): writers break the ordinary sentence Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot changed how a novel or a poem could move through time. In the same years, the magazine 新青年 and Lu Xun changed the written language of Chinese literature. They are contemporaneous events, not a required pairing. c. 1910–30 “High modernism” is a later classroom name for a cluster of European and American experiments with form, especially in the 1910s–20s. The people in this lesson did not agree they were in a school. This lesson looks out from London, Paris, and Dublin — the usual triangle — and then notices that 1918 in Shanghai is the same year, not a sidebar assigned to make the triangle look global. Literature literature 1914 Blast The Vorticist magazine appeared in London. Then the First World War arrived, which the magazine’s type had been rehearsing as noise. 1916 Portrait Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man appeared in book form. 1918 狂人日記 / 新青年 Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary” was printed in New Youth, vol. 4, no. 5. Vernacular Chinese became a literary event. 1919 May Fourth Student protests in Beijing against the Versailles settlement’s handling of Shandong. A political date that literary history also has to hold. 1922 Ulysses / Waste Land Joyce published Ulysses in Paris through Shakespeare and Company; Eliot published The Waste Land in London. A year the syllabus never lets go. 1925–27 Woolf Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse. A day, a house, and a mind used as structure instead of a plot summary. The Waste Land came with notes attached When Eliot published The Waste Land in book form in 1922, he added notes. Some explain quotations; some are jokes; some have been treated as a key to a locked poem. He later said the notes began as a way to pad a slim book. Whether you believe the shrug or not, the notes are part of how the poem was sold and taught. A modernist fragment can arrive with its own apparatus. high modernism High modernism modernism Later critical name for early-twentieth-century formal experiment — fragmentation, interiority, mythic scaffolding — especially in English-language literature around 1910–30. The writers did not vote for the label. stream of consciousness A way of writing a mind in motion: associations, sensory fragments, not always a tidy paragraph. Woolf and Joyce are the usual English-language exhibits. The phrase is a critic’s tool, not a 1922 brand name. Ulysses Joyce’s 1922 novel, published in Paris by Shakespeare and Company. One day in Dublin (16 June 1904), a Homeric scaffolding, and a censorship history in the English-speaking world. The Waste Land Waste Land Eliot’s 1922 poem. Fragments, quotations, notes. Ezra Pound cut it. The notes are part of the poem’s public life, not a teacher’s appendix only. Mrs Dalloway Woolf’s 1925 novel. A day in London, a party, a war still in the body of a man who was in it. Time is the structure. Blast Short-lived Vorticist magazine, London, 1914–15, edited by Wyndham Lewis, with Pound among the contributors. Two issues. The cover is a manifesto in type. 新青年 New Youth La Jeunesse Xin Qingnian Chinese magazine, founded 1915 by Chen Duxiu (first as 青年雜誌 / Youth Magazine). The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary.” It argued for vernacular writing and a new culture in the same years Europe was calling itself modern. May Fourth 五四 May Fourth Movement 4 May 1919: student protests in Beijing against the Versailles settlement’s handling of Shandong. “May Fourth” also names a wider New Culture moment — language, gender, science, the nation — that is not a footnote to London. 狂人日記 A Madman’s Diary Diary of a Madman Lu Xun story, 1918, written in vernacular Chinese. A reader who sees cannibalism in the classical tradition. It is a modernist event in a different language politics. Shakespeare and Company Sylvia Beach’s Paris bookshop. It published Ulysses in 1922 when British and American houses would not. A shop can be a press. Bloomsbury Loose London circle (Woolfs, Bells, Keynes, Strachey, and others). Useful as an address. Misleading if you use it as a synonym for all of modernism. Vorticism London avant-garde around Lewis and Blast, briefly, just before and into the First World War. A British answer to Futurism that did not last as a movement and left a very loud magazine. vernacular Chinese 白話 baihua Written Chinese closer to speech, as opposed to classical literary Chinese. The New Culture argument was that literature had to change language, not only subject. Lu Xun’s 1918 story is a landmark in that change. Before Nineteenth-century narrative still walked the reader through time The novel and the poem, in the late nineteenth century, could still pretend that time moved in a straight sequence. Even when they doubted that, they usually guided the reader from one event to the next. The decade before 1914 was already restless — free verse, impressionism, a city speeding up — but the First World War is the fact that later readers use to explain why that sequence broke. It is not the only fact. Cities, psychoanalysis, new print, and a reading public that included more women and more students were already changing who literature was for, and how it could be written. Virginia Stephen, photographed by George Charles Beresford in 1902 — years before Mrs Dalloway. The public-domain portrait is of a young woman who had not yet written the books this lesson is about. That is useful. Modernism did not arrive fully formed in a 1922 jacket. Virginia Woolf in profile, 1902, photograph by George Charles Beresford. The era The usual syllabus clusters around 1922; Shanghai had 1918 From London and Paris the syllabus bunches around 1922: Ulysses from Sylvia Beach’s shop; The Waste Land in The Criterion and then as a book, cut by Ezra Pound. Woolf’s major novels come a few years later, but the method is in the same family — a day, a mind, a city, and a refusal to narrate as if a life were a plot summary. Stream of consciousness is the critic’s name for that method. The writers were trying to put on the page how attention actually moves: associations, sensory fragments, not always a tidy paragraph. James Joyce, photographed by C. P. Curran in 1918, while Ulysses was still appearing in parts and still unfinished. The book would be a 1922 Paris object. The face is already the one the century kept. Sepia portrait of James Joyce with glasses and a goatee, around 1918. T. S. Eliot as a young man in a study — the usual furniture of the poet as intellectual. The Waste Land (1922) is not only a study poem. It is a collage of other people’s lines, a London of the war’s aftermath, and a set of notes that became part of the work’s public life. T. S. Eliot as a young man in a study, holding a pipe. The same years, not as a required pairing: in Shanghai, 新青年 (New Youth / La Jeunesse) was arguing that Chinese literature had to change its language. The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s 「狂人日記」. A reader in that story sees cannibalism in the classical tradition. In 1919, May Fourth made the language argument a street protest as well as a magazine fight. This is not “the Asian Woolf.” It is a contemporaneous fight about vernacular writing, the nation, and who a written sentence is for — happening while Eliot was assembling fragments and Joyce was finishing a day in Dublin. 新青年 4:5, May 1918. The contents list includes 魯迅’s 「狂人日記」. The French title La Jeunesse is on the cover. A Shanghai magazine, in the same decade as Blast and Ulysses, announcing that the language of literature would have to change. Cover of New Youth magazine, volume 4 number 5, May 1918, listing 狂人日記 by 魯迅. Lu Xun, Shanghai, 24 September 1930, inscribed at age fifty. The photograph is later than “A Madman’s Diary.” It is the face that the 1918 story, and the years after May Fourth, made public. Studio portrait of Lu Xun in a light changshan, dated Shanghai, 24 September 1930. Blast, in 1914, is the London version of a public manifesto. Two issues, then a war that killed some of the people who might have kept the magazine going. High modernism is often taught as quiet interior monologue. The pink cover is a reminder that it also wanted to be a poster. People Four writers, one decade, not one school Virginia Woolf 1882–1941 Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), A Room of One’s Own (1929). She used the sentence as a record of attention: what a mind notices in a day, not a plot summary of a life. Bloomsbury is the address, not the whole explanation. Beresford’s 1902 portrait, years before the novels. James Joyce 1882–1941 Dublin on the page, published in Paris when London and New York houses were still afraid of the book. Ulysses is one day (16 June 1904), a Homeric scaffolding, and a censorship history. Shakespeare and Company was a bookshop that became a press. Curran’s 1918 photograph, while the book was still unfinished. T. S. Eliot 1888–1965 American-born, London-settled. The Waste Land is the poem the century assigned to 1922. The notes, the quotations, and Pound’s cuts are part of the object, not extras a teacher added later. A study portrait from the early career. Lu Xun 魯迅 1881–1936 Zhou Shuren. “A Madman’s Diary,” then a body of stories, essays, and translations that made vernacular literary Chinese a fact. He is in this lesson because 1918 is 1918 — not because a Western syllabus needed an Asian twin. Shanghai, 1930, later than the 1918 story. A story Two magazines, one decade, two different projects Blast 1, 1914. The word is the picture: a title used as a poster. Blast magazine cover, 1914. Put Blast next to 新青年. One is a London roar in English, two issues, then a war. The other is a Shanghai magazine that ran for years and printed a story that helped change the written language. They are not the same project. They share a decade in which people decided the old sentence was part of the problem. That is enough of a reason to put them in one lesson. It is not a reason to make one the key to the other. After How these books became a teaching canon By the 1930s the experiments had become a canon in some places and a target in others. Woolf died in 1941; Joyce the same year; Lu Xun in 1936; Eliot lived long enough to become a monument. The after of high modernism is partly a teaching machine: 1922 as a fetish year, stream of consciousness as a worksheet. The after is also every later writer who inherited the broken narrative sequence and had to decide whether to restore it. If this archive later takes a Thursday to a different literature, it will not be to complete a set. It will be because another year also happened. A question A question to keep asking When a syllabus says “1922,” whose 1918 was dropped to make the year look clean? T. S. Eliot reads The Waste Land (recording) The text is 1922. Recordings circulate legally via libraries and the Poetry Foundation’s page; this is not a film of 1922. James Joyce reads from Finnegans Wake (Anna Livia Plurabelle) Internet Archive copy of Joyce’s own recording. Later than Ulysses; still his voice.

title: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio

text: French New Wave (c. 1958–64): the camera leaves the studio Young French critics attacked the polished studio cinema they called the tradition of quality, then made their own films in real streets with lighter cameras. A 1959–62 burst of features, and a magazine that had already trained an audience, gave the press a name: Nouvelle Vague. c. 1958–64 “Nouvelle Vague” was a press label before it was a school. The people in this lesson argued in Cahiers du Cinéma, learned at the Cinémathèque as much as at the official film school IDHEC, then made films that did not look like the tradition de qualité they had been attacking. This lesson looks out from Paris. Free Cinema, the Japanese New Wave, and cinéma vérité were happening in the same years. They are not assigned peers. Taiwan New Cinema is a later relative that borrowed the “new cinema” idea, not a 1960 contemporary. Film film 1951–54 Cahiers Cahiers du Cinéma was founded in 1951. Critics were already picking up cameras before the press had a label for them. 1959 Cannes Les Quatre Cents Coups and Hiroshima mon amour. The jump cuts were also a way to shorten the film Godard and editor Cécile Decugis shortened Breathless by cutting inside shots, not only between them. The jump cut is now taught as a philosophy of time. It was also a way to lose running time without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true: a device can be an idea and a solution to a reel that was too long. Nouvelle Vague New Wave French New Wave Press name, late 1950s, for a cluster of mostly young French directors who had often been critics first. A useful label, and a bad census of everyone who was making films that way. tradition de qualité tradition of quality Tradition of Quality cinéma de qualité Truffaut’s hostile name for the polished, literary, studio-bound French cinema of the 1940s–50s that Cahiers wanted to replace. “Quality” here is an insult. ciné-clubs ciné-club Postwar French film societies that screened and argued over films outside the commercial circuit. A training ground before a camera was a job. IDHEC The official French film school (Institut des hautes études cinématographiques). The New Wave’s joke was that you could learn more in the dark at the Cinémathèque than in its classrooms. Cinémathèque Cinémathèque française The Cinémathèque française, the archive and screening room associated with Henri Langlois. For the Cahiers critics it was a school: Hollywood and Europe, night after night. Henri Langlois Co-founder of the Cinémathèque française. The programmers’ programmer: he showed the films the school and the industry had filed as disposable. André Bazin Critic and co-founder of Cahiers du Cinéma. A father figure the younger writers both used and argued with. Cahiers du Cinéma Cahiers French film magazine, founded 1951. Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rivette, and Rohmer wrote there. The magazine trained an audience and then supplied directors. politique des auteurs auteur theory Cahiers argument: a director can be the author of a film the way a novelist is the author of a book — including in Hollywood, if the films have a signature. In English this hardened into “auteur theory.” It was a polemic, not a law of nature. auteur The director-as-author, in the Cahiers sense. A fighting word before it was a festival brochure word. Alfred Hitchcock Hitchcock Hollywood director the Cahiers critics treated as an author, not a genre mechanic. The insult to French “quality” was the point. Howard Hawks Hawks Hollywood director claimed by Cahiers as an auteur. Hawks, Hitchcock, Nicholas Ray: the American names in the French fight. Nicholas Ray Hollywood director (Rebel Without a Cause and others) whom Cahiers treated as a signature, not a studio employee. jump cut jump cuts An edit that skips a bit of time inside a continuous shot, so the image jerks. Breathless made the device famous as style, not as a mistake to be hidden. Cameflex Éclair Cameflex Eclair Cameflex Lightweight French 35mm camera (Éclair). New Wave crews used cameras like this because they could leave the studio. available light Shooting with the light already in the street or room, rather than a studio grid. An aesthetic with a budget attached. location shooting Filming in real streets and rooms instead of sets. Italian neorealism had already done this; Paris made it look like a choice and a generation. Left Bank Later grouping of filmmakers including Varda, Resnais, and Marker — often more essayistic than the Cahiers men. Useful as a map, and too neat if you treat it as a wall. Georges de Beauregard Producer of Breathless and other early New Wave features. The movement had a checkbook, not only a manifesto. Pierre Braunberger Producer who backed several New Wave and Left Bank films. Another name for the fact that cheap was not free. François Truffaut Truffaut Critic, then director. “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” (1954); Les Quatre Cents Coups (1959). The man who attacked the tradition of quality later became, himself, a kind of tradition. Jean-Luc Godard Godard Critic, then director. À bout de souffle (1960) is the film people mean when they say “jump cut.” The longer fact is a director who treated cinema as an argument. Claude Chabrol Chabrol Cahiers critic, then director. Le Beau Serge (1958) is often called the first New Wave feature — a provincial story, not a Paris postcard. Jacques Rivette Rivette Cahiers critic, then director. Paris nous appartient (1961) is a Paris of plots and rooms, longer-breathed than the jump-cut cliché. Éric Rohmer Eric Rohmer Rohmer Cahiers critic and later editor, then director of talkative moral tales. In the 1959–62 burst he is already in the magazine’s inner room. Agnès Varda Agnes Varda Varda Photographer first, then filmmaker. La Pointe Courte (1955) is often called a New Wave film before the name. Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962) is the later public proof she was not a guest. Alain Resnais Resnais Left Bank director. Hiroshima mon amour (1959) is a literary, time-tangled film from the same Cannes season as The 400 Blows — not a Cahiers boys’ night out. Chris Marker Marker Essay-filmmaker of the Left Bank. A name on the map even when a given year’s famous titles are someone else’s. Jacques Demy Demy Director of Lola (1961). A musical intelligence in the same years; often parked beside Varda, which is geography and a marriage, not a full account. Louis Malle Malle Director of Les Amants (1958). Adjacent to the burst: a scandal about adult desire, not a Cahiers calling card. Jean-Pierre Léaud Léaud Actor; Antoine Doinel in Les Quatre Cents Coups and later Truffaut films. A new face who became a recurring one. Jean Seberg Seberg American actress; the American in Paris in À bout de souffle. Breathless without her face is a different object. Jean-Paul Belmondo Belmondo Actor; the petty criminal in À bout de souffle. A new star who looked like he had walked in from the street. Anna Karina Karina Actress and Godard’s collaborator in the films just after Breathless. A face the New Wave kept walking back to. Raoul Coutard Cinematographer of Breathless, Jules et Jim, and many other New Wave films. Handheld, available light, a camera that could walk. Cécile Decugis Cecile Decugis Editor of Breathless. The jump cuts are hers as well as Godard’s. Marguerite Duras Novelist and screenwriter of Hiroshima mon amour. The literary half of a film the Cahiers story likes to file under directors only. Antoine Doinel The boy in Les Quatre Cents Coups, played by Jean-Pierre Léaud. Truffaut returned to him. A character, not a mascot. Une certaine tendance du cinéma français Truffaut’s 1954 Cahiers essay attacking the tradition of quality. A fight about scripts, adaptation, and who authors a film. Le Beau Serge Chabrol, 1958. Often cited as the first New Wave feature: a return to a provincial town, shot away from the studio comfort the essay had mocked. Les Quatre Cents Coups The 400 Blows 400 Blows Truffaut, 1959. Next to the New Wave, not inside its magazine. La Pointe Courte Varda, 1955. A fishing village and a marriage, often called a New Wave film before the name existed. Free Cinema British mid-1950s documentary movement (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson and others): short films, everyday subjects, a manifesto. Contemporaneous, not a French export. British New Wave British late-1950s/early-1960s features that grew out of Free Cinema and the kitchen-sink plays: working-class rooms, location shooting, a different class accent. Lindsay Anderson British Free Cinema and later feature director. A name on the British side of the same years. Karel Reisz British Free Cinema and New Wave director. Tony Richardson British Free Cinema and New Wave director. Japanese New Wave Nuberu Bagu nūberu bāgu Japanese 1960s directors (Oshima, Imamura, Teshigahara and others) breaking with studio form. The name borrows the French phrase. The films do not. Nagisa Oshima Oshima Japanese New Wave director. Cruel Story of Youth (1960) is the usual first citation in a short list. Shohei Imamura Imamura Japanese New Wave director. Pigs and Battleships (1961) is one place the studio system starts to look breakable. Hiroshi Teshigahara Teshigahara Japanese New Wave director. Woman in the Dunes (1964) is the international title people remember. cinéma vérité cinema verite A documentary idea of the same years: lightweight cameras, direct sound, people talking in the present. Chronicle of a Summer (Rouch and Morin, 1961) is the usual French exhibit. Jean Rouch Anthropologist-filmmaker; with Edgar Morin, Chronicle of a Summer (1961). Cinéma vérité’s most cited French name. Edgar Morin Sociologist; with Jean Rouch, Chronicle of a Summer. Chronicle of a Summer Chronique d’un été Rouch and Morin, 1961 (Chronique d’un été). Paris people, a lightweight camera, the present tense as a method. Italian neorealism neorealism Postwar Italian films that took ruined streets as a set. The New Wave’s location habit has this earlier cousin. Cannes The festival that, in 1959, made Les Quatre Cents Coups an international event. A prize is not a movement, but it is how a movement gets a date journalists can print. New Hollywood U.S. late-1960s/1970s studio crash and youth-market turn. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the usual bridge sentence from the New Wave. A later effect, not a twin. Bonnie and Clyde Arthur Penn, 1967. The sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete. Taiwan New Cinema 1980s Taiwanese film movement (Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others). A later cousin in the family of “new cinemas,” not a 1960 contemporary. Hou Hsiao-hsien Taiwan New Cinema director. A later name, for the after — not a 1959 peer. Edward Yang Taiwan New Cinema director. Again: 1980s, a cousin, not a contemporary. Before A fight with studio “quality,” a magazine, and a camera light enough to carry The French cinema the young critics wanted to replace had a name they gave it: tradition de qualité, or cinéma de qualité — well-upholstered literary adaptations, studio craft, a finished look that felt, to them, dead. François Truffaut’s 1954 Cahiers du Cinéma essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” is the fight in print. The other half of the fight was the politique des auteurs. A director, even in Hollywood, could be an author. Alfred Hitchcock counted. So did Howard Hawks. So did Nicholas Ray. The insult to the French studio system was the point: if those American directors were authors, the polished French adapters were not. They had learned the argument in rooms that were not IDHEC, the official French film school. Postwar ciné-clubs trained an audience to argue. The Cinémathèque française, under Henri Langlois, showed Hollywood and Europe as if the distinction did not matter. André Bazin’s Cahiers, founded in 1951, hired the arguers: Truffaut, Jean-Luc Godard, Claude Chabrol, Jacques Rivette, Éric Rohmer. The official school existed. The joke — and it was only half a joke — was that you learned more in Langlois’s dark than in a curriculum. An Éclair Cameflex, the kind of relatively light 35mm camera Paris rental houses such as Chevereau supplied. New Wave form is often taught as an idea. It is also equipment that could be carried into a street. An Éclair Cameflex 35mm movie camera on a tripod, labeled Eclair Paris and Chevereau. They were not the first people to want a camera outside. Italian neorealism had already taken the war’s rubble as a set. What was new in Paris was the combination: critics who became directors, a magazine that had already trained an audience, faster film stock, lighter cameras, and producers — Georges de Beauregard, Pierre Braunberger — willing to bet on a low budget that looked like a choice. The era What the films looked like once they left the studio The look is easy to list and easy to turn into a costume. Location shooting. Jump cuts. Available light. Young non-stars or new faces: Jean-Pierre Léaud, Jean Seberg, Jean-Paul Belmondo, Anna Karina. Handheld cameras, Raoul Coutard walking them through traffic. A 1959–62 burst in which it suddenly seemed that everyone who had written for Cahiers, and several people who had not, had a feature. Louis Malle’s Les Amants (1958) sits beside that cluster. The line leaks. That is why it is a map and not a membership list. The Latin Quarter as a working street, not a back lot. New Wave location shooting made Paris look like a place people already lived — which is why the city in these films still feels like itself, and why a production still needed permits, light, and luck. Later classrooms will call this a philosophy. It was also a way to shorten a film without reshooting Paris. Both things can be true. The person is not in doubt: a director who was already working when the magazine men picked up cameras. Agnès Varda, short dark hair, standing with another woman on a wooden deck over water. A later photograph of a portable camera on a tripod. This is not a 1959 production still. It is here because the New Wave’s bet — that a lighter camera changes who gets to shoot, and where — did not stay in Paris. The equipment traveled. The date of this picture is later than the era. The idea is the era’s. Children looking through a professional motion-picture camera on a tripod, with an adult nearby. Elsewhere The same years, different arguments In Britain, Free Cinema’s shorts and manifesto — Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz, Tony Richardson — had already argued for everyday subjects and a camera that did not owe the studio a polished lie. The British New Wave features that followed are contemporaneous, not a French franchise. In Japan, Nagisa Oshima, Shohei Imamura, Hiroshi Teshigahara and others were breaking studio form; the phrase nūberu bāgu borrows the French name and then goes its own way. Cinéma vérité — Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin’s Chronicle of a Summer (1961) — is another French argument of the same years: not fiction’s jump cut, but a claim on the present tense. These are contemporaneous arguments, not a ranking with France at the top. After Later filmmakers borrowed the methods, and a later cinema borrowed the name American studios in the late 1960s needed a younger audience and had lost the old Production Code’s certainty. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the sentence film histories use to connect Paris to New Hollywood. The connection is real and incomplete. A lot of other things — television, the draft, the collapse of the studio system’s weekly habit — were part of the same American turn. Taiwan New Cinema, in the 1980s — Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others — is sometimes filed as another “new wave.” It is a later relative: a different state, a different language politics, a different argument with its own studios. It does not belong on the 1958–64 timeline except as a reminder that the French name traveled, and that travel is not the same as origin. A question A question to keep asking If the director is the author, whose names have to wait in the credits? The 400 Blows — Criterion film page Legal home-video edition. This capsule does not link a pirated full film. Breathless — Criterion film page À bout de souffle, 1960. Again: the licensed edition, not a rip. Cléo from 5 to 7 — Criterion film page Varda, 1962. Watch a legal copy. Hiroshima Mon Amour — Criterion film page Resnais, 1959. Licensed edition. BFI — Free Cinema Britain, same years: a manifesto and a set of shorts, not a French franchise.
